c371d06a5231e17d: How do you think you're going to die?

If you go by the current statistics for deaths in the US, it's reasonable to expect that cancer or heart disease will eventually get you. But OpenAI Foundation board member and Alignment Research Center Executive Director Paul Cristiano thinks we should all be worried about another major mortality risk. Speaking at a lecture series this week, Cristiano bluntly told the audience in a Toronto Convention Center, "I think for most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident."

In the opening lecture of a three-part series, Cristiano outlined his worries about the risk of an impending "AI takeover." He defined that as a situation where goal-pursuing AI systems "call the shots in the same sense that humans today call the shots and what happens on Earth" and where any human trying to stop them "would be as ineffective as if you or me was trying to stop the US military." Such a situation would likely lead to mass death and perhaps uninhabitable environments for humans, Cristiano said.

b5e375717c051ebb: Solo, Mozilla's LLM-powered website builder and hosting service, is shutting down. All sites and data will be deleted on November 30.

Mozilla launched Solo in December 2023 as a "Mozilla Innovation Project," aimed at helping sole traders to build themselves a webpage for their services. Some 54,000 people used its LLM to build pages, and relied on Mozilla to host them – complete with custom domain names.

Well, not any more. Now the Soloist.ai homepage says: "We've made the difficult decision to close Solo. We have appreciated all of your support building and growing this product, and the feedback we've received from all of you. Solo will cease operations on Nov 30, 2026."

Users now have just over two weeks left to find a new home for their pages, although Mozilla says it first notified them on October 1. According to the support FAQ, users can download a ZIP containing an HTML export, contact form and newsletter submissions, and a CSV linking to their images.

The images themselves must be downloaded separately. Domains purchased through Solo Domains must also be moved to Name.com, with Mozilla handling the transfer after users create an account and supply its code. So much for having the fiddly bits taken care of.

It also points at a couple of other bot-based site-generating services – in case all this feels like a bit too much. We suspect that for the sort of technophobes that this was aimed at, it very probably will.

Mozilla told The Register: "Experimentation is an important part of Mozilla's mission to make the internet better and give people more choice and control online. Sometimes, that means making the decision to bring a product to an end. Solo will officially shut down on November 30, 2026. We initially notified customers on October 1, providing a 60-day transition period, and have been offering support to help them download their website data and migrate their domains purchased via Solo Domains to another hosting provider."

It seems that some 54,000 users were not enough to keep it going, and we can see that this would cost money to keep running. An HTML export is a start, though the FAQ doesn't explain how much work it will take to get a complete, functioning site running elsewhere.

Buried in the dark recesses of the web is this vulture's own nearly 30-year-old homepage, created using a mixture of Claris Home Page (which was excellent) and Microsoft FrontPage (ever so slightly less so). We saw what a mess machine-generated web content was back then, and thanks to LLMs, we suspect it is almost infinitely worse now.

Mozilla might have made a few bucks by finding a commercial partner to take on its users, and perhaps through them offer a paid site-and-domain transfer service. As we noted last year, it seems not to have negotiated anything with KaiOSTech, which maintains and sells what used to be the formerly FOSS FirefoxOS for use on low-end smartphones.

3aef5da08ef01001: Two email addresses used to send bomb threats that disrupted thousands of Italian schools this week were found exposed in infostealer logs for over a year, experts say.

Researchers at Hudson Rock looked into the two university email addresses used to send the bomb threats. One, from Egypt’s Kafrelsheikh University, was scooped up by Vidar – a cybercrime tool that steals saved account credentials and passwords from an infected computer and leaks them to attackers – as far back as October 2021. The other, from Taiwan's Dayeh University, was found among the 284 million addresses included in the massive AlienTXTBASE infostealer dump, dated February 2025.
The experts said that the two addresses in infostealer logs do not strictly mean that those behind the bomb threats gained access to the accounts using the previous infostealer compromise.

However, it suggests that there was ample time for the universities and Microsoft, which both universities used for authentication, to take action against the accounts that they should have been aware were appearing in infostealer logs.
Modern threat intelligence has made infostealer logs highly visible.
"Both findings place credential exposure well before the disruption, creating a substantial window in which exposed access could have been investigated and secured," Hudson Rock said.

The researchers said that they would need access to details such as the email headers, and data from email providers, including sign-in events and audit records, that could show them more about who sent the email and from what session.

Understanding whether the sender authenticated into the account could rule out spoofing, but would not in itself provide proof that the sender used a corresponding password taken from an infostealer log, Hudson Rock noted. There are many ways to get around password-based authentication.

The researchers said that in any case where a credential is detected among infostealer logs, the organizations responsible for those accounts must contain them, revoke their access, rotate secrets, and go looking for suspicious activity.
"The disruption illustrates why credential exposure deserves attention beyond fraud and data theft," the researchers said.
"An account associated with an ordinary university user can become a means of reaching schools, frightening families, and consuming emergency resources."
The threats
Around 6,300 of Italy's 7,476 state schools received fake bomb threat emails between November 11-12, although only around 390 of them evacuated their respective buildings.
The emails contained messaging such as "we will annihilate you," and "we will carry out genocide against Italians," and mention of a "powerful explosive device… with a remote trigger."

Early reports suggested that the emails came from a Taiwanese email address and were signed by a "Mikhail Andropov, leader of the Vilayat of Misoginistan" – a fictitious state or region roughly mapping to "the land of Misogyny," with "vilayat" meaning an administrative region of the Ottoman Empire.

Various theories have been reported about the identity of the sender, ranging from a teacher based in the Philippines whose email was compromised to a Russia-backed disruption operation. Neither are confirmed. Russia denied any involvement.
Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said on Thursday evening that there was no credence to the emails, and that whoever was behind the coordinated hoax sought to invoke chaos across the country.
"To date, there is no evidence of a concrete danger," she said, ANSA reported. "These messages aren't intended to shock, they're intended to scare.

"Those who write them are primarily seeking our fear, wasted days, suspicion, and chaos. Investigators and the judiciary, along with their European colleagues, are working to determine who is behind them."
Schools in France, Ireland, Northern Ireland, and Scotland also received similar emails this week. None of the respective police forces believed the threats were legitimate.
Hundreds of schools across the Republic of Ireland received the emails, as did news organizations such as RTÉ, which evacuated its Donnybrook campus, disrupting scheduled programming.
Around 300 schools in Northern Ireland received bomb threats, although the PSNI said these were being treated as a hoax, and that the risk to the public was deemed low.
Likewise, Police Scotland confirmed around 1,000 schools were affected by the email campaign and that the threats weren’t believed to be credible.

In France, three school districts confirmed they received similar threats. Separately, domestic and international rail travel, including Eurostar services to London, were interrupted on Thursday following bomb threats made to Calais-Fréthun station.
The latest wave of threats follows similar happenings at other types of organizations in recent weeks, including airline operators, air traffic controllers, and blood banks.

At least 34 flights across various operators in Europe were affected earlier this month. Some were forced into unplanned landings, such as an Aer Lingus flight which pulled up to a French air base instead of its intended target of Rome.
Military fighter jets were also scrambled to escort others in Italian and Austrian airspace. ®

c7ce2f492cafa072: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysian singer Aina Abdul stands a strong chance of winning the inaugural Eurovision Song Contest Asia 2026 in Bangkok on Saturday, Malaysia's five-member jury panel said.
However, they warned she faces stiff competition, particularly from South Korea, Thailand, the Philippines, Bangladesh and Nepal.
Chief Malaysian juror, composer and producer AG Coco said a winner must deliver a memorable performance that stands out.
"Aina always steps up and does better each time, and that means her chances of winning the contest are really good," he said.
"As a singer-songwriter who always sets a benchmark in local entertainment, Aina must come up with a good, strong song, and Bluest Sky is such a song."
AG, who has judged several international and local music contests, said Aina's biggest rivals are from the Philippines, Thailand and South Korea.
"If she goes all out and surprises everyone with a performance that resonates with the crowd, I'm sure she's got a great chance of victory," he said.
Fellow juror, producer and composer Justin Seow, judging the competition for the first time, said tonight that Aina must put up a tough fight against strong entrants from the Philippines and Nepal.

"Having watched the rehearsals, I must say that the Philippines and Nepal entrants are really good, too. It's going to be a great show, and what's most important for Aina is giving fans something different once again," Seow said.
He said the award-winning singer is known for pushing boundaries and raising benchmarks among Malaysian artistes.
"I've watched Aina in action in many concerts, and each time she really surprises us with her thinking out of the box, and planning each performance well," he said.
Concert promoter and event organiser Iman Tang said Aina is a "rock-solid" competitor with a good chance of winning, though she must be wary of "dark horses" Bangladesh and Nepal.

"This annual, prestigious concert is known to set benchmarks really high, and I'm confident Aina has what it takes to reach the very top. She is known for her superb showmanship and production values, not to mention her singing capabilities," Tang said.
Commercial and film director Bobby Husaini and Berita Harian senior entertainment news and projects editor Shamshul Azree Samshir were equally optimistic about Aina's prospects.
Shamshul said: "Aina has proven herself again and again, that she's a tireless performer who always steps out of her comfort zone to give music lovers plenty of surprises.
"This is a very crucial factor for any competitor, that is to be entertaining and out of the ordinary, as well as giving audiences an unpredictably good act," he said.
"Aina's got it all, plus superb vocals. Even if she doesn't win, she's really going to put Malaysian music on the world map."
Bobby said: "What we look for is originality, and while it's not going to be an easy road to the top, I'm optimistic that Aina will go far and capture the imagination of audiences and jurors alike."
Yesterday, Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim wished Aina, Malaysia's first representative at the contest, well.
In a Facebook post, Anwar said her participation showed that Malaysian talent and creative works could reach greater heights and compete internationally.
Aina's selection was announced during the 40th Anugerah Juara Lagu (AJL40) on Aug 15.
She will perform her song Bluest Sky—released on Oct 9 and described by her as a "love letter" to someone special—against entrants from 10 other Asian countries.

The track has drawn positive reactions from international listeners, and supporters are confident the 33-year-old from Seremban, Negri Sembilan—best known for hits such as Sumpah and Sepi—can deliver a strong performance.
On Nov 10, Aina wrote on Threads that preparing for the contest had given her a taste of what it is like to be an athlete.
"Thank you to my beloved fans for accompanying me on my journey. I'm so touched—I'll do my very best, okay?" she said.

Under the competition's voting system, each participating country is represented by five professional jurors whose scores make up 50 per cent of the final results, with the remaining 50 per cent decided by public vote.
The panel watches the dress rehearsals together to judge the artistic merit and overall performance of each entry before submitting individual rankings through an online voting system.
Official broadcaster TV3 will air the Eurovision Song Contest Asia 2026 live at 9.30pm tomorrow, with simultaneous streaming on Tonton.

bc9e424becdbff07: Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day.

On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System, which Microsoft describes as a “general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode.” By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System.
Turning a Windows defense against itself

The attack exploits the interaction of CLFS, Windows Defender, and Windows file permissions. The exploit uses Windows Defender to open a log file created by a standard user by calling ServerMpUpdateEngineSignature, a legitimate Defender function for processing antivirus signature updates.

aaecb86ebb696688: HPE is pitching high performance compute customers with hybrid configurations of its Cray Supercomputing Storage Systems built for faster throughput, along with a Rack Management Controller that monitors cooling systems.

The hardware giant already supplies its Cray Supercomputing Storage Systems E2000 in all-flash, all-disk, tiered and hybrid configurations, but - we're told - the latest combination offers up to 41 percent more data throughput per storage rack.
The E2000 line embeds the Lustre open-source parallel file system, and is generally intended to fit NVMe Gen 5 solid-state drive (SSD) building blocks.
For the refreshed hybrid configurations, HPE is combining SSDs with new 32 TB SAS-4 (24 Gb/s SAS) HDDs and new enclosures supporting 74 or 100 drives.

HPE says it'll deliver up to 116 GB/s of read throughput and 92 GB/s of write throughput per rack, with up to 32 percent more usable storage capacity per rack for expansion to support the growing size of datasets in HPC, especially where sites are mixing AI and traditional simulation-style workloads.

One of the reasons behind these new hybrid configurations could be the ballooning cost of storage, caused by the relentless demand for AI infrastructure skewing the price of components such as memory and many other things. But prices for silicon-based NAND flash SSDs are growing faster than those of good old hard drives, as our colleagues at Blocks & Files reported.

HPE says that as demand for data-intensive workloads grows, prices for large SSDs have soared. The company claims the new hybrid configurations let research institutions and national laboratories spend less on storage and put that money toward compute node purchases, without giving up on the performance they need.

“When making long-term investments in environments where advanced workloads are rapidly evolving, our customers want scalable, dense, and flexible systems to help them address dynamic shifts in requirements," said Trish Damkroger, HPE senior veep for HPC and AI Infrastructure Solutions.
The latest hybrid configurations are expected to go on sale in early 2027.

HPE's other introduction is a Rack Management Controller, providing what HPE calls "intelligent liquid cooling” via real-time monitoring, leak detection and automated control features. It integrates with HPE Supercomputing Management Software to gather telemetry and provide control.

Several platform-specific versions will be offered, each tailored to different rack-scale systems. Support will launch with HPE's own Cray Supercomputing GX5000 infrastructure, naturally, with versions for Nvidia’s NVL72 and AMD’s Helion and Helios kit to follow.
The Rack Management Controller will be available for HPE’s kit in March 2027, with support for AMD and Nvidia expected to follow in June. ®

9b2b7d8187cec4fb: Microsoft 365 services are slowly recovering from a prolonged outage that has handed critics of single-vendor dependence a particularly unwelcome case study.

Ever wondered what it would be like if your IT supplier abruptly pulled the plug? Perhaps the result of a mood swing by an unpredictable political leader? For affected Microsoft customers, the disruption has offered an unwelcome preview. Email? Gone. Messaging with Teams? Iffy. Collaboration? Nope.

The list of problems in what Microsoft delicately called a "Service Degradation" is breathtaking. The company put the incident's start at 1826 GMT on November 12. Exchange Online fell over. Viewing recently used files in the Microsoft 365 application was problematic. Copilot threw a wobbly. Microsoft 365 Education was affected (unfortunate, considering the changes the company has made), and so on.

At 1401 GMT on November 13, Microsoft reported: "We're continuing to see improvements in service availability," but the damage has surely been done. If the outage halted work at your organization, then questions will have to be asked.
Even Microsoft's rivals had some sympathy for the engineers and administrators dealing with the problems.
Jos Poortvliet, co-founder of Nextcloud, told The Register: "Mistakes happen in the IT industry. This holds true for companies of all sizes, including us. Our heart goes out to all the admins today.

"This incident shows how dependent organizations are on a single ecosystem. Especially in critical infrastructure, monopolies are increasing the risk of stalling businesses globally if an incident occurs.

"When everything is hanging on a single vendor, companies can't switch providers quickly to get back up and running, or have a second setup as backup, or pull the plug when under attack and keep working air-gapped."

Similarly, Civo CEO Mark Boost noted that IT whoopsies were a way of life. "Every technology provider will experience failures," he said. "The real concern isn't that Microsoft has suffered an outage. It's that we've allowed so much of our critical infrastructure to become concentrated in the hands of so few companies, creating enormous single points of failure."

Dame Chi Onwurah, chair of the Commons Science and Technology Committee, also commented: "The global Microsoft outage only serves to highlight once again the lack of resilience in the UK's digital infrastructure, and the dangers that this dependency can pose to our security, economy and public services."

This week, Microsoft warned users to treat its unsupported Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 as "permanently vulnerable." Moving to Exchange Online brings its own dependencies, however. Beyond any compensation claims, Microsoft may face awkward conversations about those dependencies when contracts come up for renewal.

And there are alternatives. Although perhaps not so extreme as the measures overheard by one vulture in a German shared workspace: "Germany's love of the fax machine – we are finally getting our chance to shine! Our British colleagues cannot email; we have reverted to the natural way of the fax."
What a time to be alive. ®

68acf9d9af310deb: JAKARTA: Indonesia's upper house of parliament will pick the country's new vice president on Dec 2, its speaker said on Friday, after the dramatic resignation of Gibran Rakabuming Raka, the president's deputy and the son of his predecessor.

Gibran's resignation this week, which analysts say could widen the gulf between President Prabowo Subianto and former president Joko Widodo, followed a month of increasing political pressure from lawmakers after Indonesia's top courts ruled that he had inadequate education credentials to run for the job.
Speaker Ahmad Muzani said the upper house, which is tasked by law with appointing the new vice president, would now send a letter to Prabowo requesting that he submit two names for the job.
The house has also formed a team of 36 lawmakers to verify the candidates' credentials, Muzani said. It was not immediately clear which names Prabowo would submit.
On Thursday, Gibran said his resignation was a personal decision and unrelated to issues pertaining to his education credentials.

Gibran, 39, was elected alongside Prabowo in the 2024 election. Critics accused his father, Widodo, better known as Jokowi, of meddling in the process by influencing a court decision that changed the election rules, enabling Gibran to stand.
Analysts believe Gibran's resignation could stoke further political turbulence and lock Jokowi and Prabowo into a bitter rivalry.
Jokowi defeated Prabowo in two presidential elections, in 2014 and 2019. During Jokowi's second term, he made Prabowo his defence minister and tacitly supported the latter's 2024 presidential run.
On Thursday, however, both Jokowi and Gibran struck a conciliatory tone and said they would continue to support Prabowo.
Gibran, in a video address to volunteers shown by news channel Kompas TV, said he would not be in opposition even as an outsider to Prabowo's administration.
"I only have one message: Please, inside or outside government, we still have to support the president," he said.

Analysts said another sign of the gulf between Prabowo and Jokowi was last week's police revelation of an inquiry into suspected illegal wiretapping by four senior police officials, including former police chief Listyo Sigit Prabowo, who is widely seen as a Jokowi loyalist.
Police said on Thursday they had enough initial evidence to pursue treason charges against the four suspects for wiretapping Prabowo, other politicians, activists and journalists.
Reuters has been unable to reach the suspects for comment.

ecc31cde59fd01c7: Arm's Lorenzo Stoakes isn't quitting Linux kernel development, though he's stepping back from some of the patch-review work he used to handle.
Stoakes is a principal software engineer at Arm and he's a busy chap. Aside from writing the forthcoming book The Linux Memory Manager, in his CV [PDF], he says:

"I hold four maintainerships: memory mapping, memory mapping (locking), memory mapping (madvise) – essentially the entirety of the userland API to memory management – and the reverse mapping which connects physical to virtual memory."
Even so, he plans to soon be doing a little less. Earlier this week he posted an email to the Linux kernel mailing list to say that he was planning to drop some of his workload.

"Given the current throughput in the kernel resulting from AI-generated series, I unfortunately lack the bandwidth to generally be able to offer review except in those areas I maintain. […] Apologies for doing this, but given the current trends I'd like to do something to make my inbox a little more manageable."
As it happens, this came just the day after the Paramount Penguin himself said that he saw signs that the AI patch tide was "starting to turn."
"I am retaining my maintainerships and have no plans on giving those up, I just want my inbox to be less horrendous.
"And yeah, AI is part of the reason; in general, it's gone from 'once a week' to 'daily' to 'half of what I see in review'.
"But the AI wave is hitting [memory management] across the board, really."

"I have a habit of burning myself out over weekends and evenings – you can see my involvement on a thread talking about that here - which gives you a sense of my views if you read back through that thread."
At the Open Source Summit last month, the Reg FOSS desk joined the "Ask the Expert" session with Greg Kroah-Hartman, and he too expressed worrying sentiments:

"The onslaught of the LLM-generated patches… we don't have enough people to review them all… We need more reviewers. We don't have enough. All of the maintainers are burnt out, and we have been for ten years."
"I want to go down to two Long Term Support releases – four, maximum. Six is too many. We're too busy. We don't have the manpower. It’s crazy."
On Red Hat's model of offering 10 years of support for products with a given version of the kernel:
"Debian does it right. Debian and Yocto run the world. I've argued for years that the RHEL and SLES model is broken. That's why I don't work for SUSE any more." ®
6e39a19b3ab1b2f4: JEERUSALEM: Israeli prime ministerial hopeful Gadi Eisenkot called on Friday for respect for the country's Arab minority after caretaker premier Benjamin Netanyahu and other right-wing figures sought to delegitimise the community's lawmakers by linking them to Hamas.

Two Arab-majority parties, Raam and the Joint List, secured a combined 19 seats in last month's election, winning nearly a sixth of the 120-seat parliament and potentially emerging as kingmakers in efforts by Eisenkot to form a government.
"Arab citizens of Israel are an integral part of the Israeli story," Eisenkot wrote on X on Friday.

"The attempt to marginalise them and vilify them collectively is a profound violation of the principles of civic responsibility. It dishonours Israel's Declaration of Independence and the values we take pride in as a Jewish and democratic state," he added.
Netanyahu and his allies have repeatedly criticised leaders of Arab parties for refusing to describe Hamas as a "terror group" following its unprecedented Oct 7, 2023 attack on Israel.

All leaders of Arab parties have condemned the attack, in which Arab Israelis -- descendants of Palestinians who remained in what became Israel in 1948, and who now form more than 20% of the population -- were also among those killed.
Netanyahu has also repeatedly alleged electoral fraud by Arab-majority parties, but electoral authorities have rejected the claims.

In a speech at the inauguration of the new parliament this week, Netanyahu lamented that the two Arab lists refuse to recognise Israel as a Jewish state, although Raam leader Mansour Abbas has done so in the past.
He further claimed that they sought to establish either an "Islamic state" or a "nationalist Palestinian state".
During the same ceremony, national security minister Itamar Ben Gvir heckled Joint List leader Youssef Jabareen during his oath of allegiance, accusing him of having "pledged allegiance to Hamas".

"It is entirely legitimate to disagree with representatives of the Arab parties, even to strongly disapprove of some of them. But it is neither legitimate nor acceptable to malign an entire community, and I will not allow it," Eisenkot said.

President Isaac Herzog tasked Eisenkot with forming a new government on Sunday after consultations in which a majority of political parties, including the two Arab lists, recommended him for the role.
But one of Eisenkot's right-wing allies, Avigdor Liberman has said he will back out of the coalition if Israeli-Arabs are part of it.
If Eisenkot fails to form a government within 28 days, he may request a 14-day extension. Should he still fall short, the mandate would pass to another lawmaker, most likely Netanyahu.

72a74addd2326b9e: Late in his blitz to salvage Republicans' midterm fortunes, United States Vice-President JD Vance has shifted strategy. He talked less about President Donald Trump and more about the issues that define his own political identity.

Vance argued the case for Republicans, who lost control of Congress, almost exclusively through the lens of his policy portfolio, according to a Reuters review of half a dozen speeches since the Republican convention in September.
He bypassed Trump's signature policies, including the Iran war and deportations, as polls showed the president's sagging popularity dragging down Republican office-seekers.
The change was deliberate, according to two people familiar with the strategy.
Vance and his advisers saw the issues he championed — economic nationalism, foreign policy restraint and public safety — as politically potent subjects he could address with authority.
The shift offered an early glimpse of how the 42-year-old vice-president could chart his own course as Republicans begin looking beyond Trump.
Vance hasn't said whether he will run for president in 2028, and Trump hasn't endorsed him or anyone else.
But Vance is viewed as a leading potential contender who some Republican officials say will need to inherit much of Trump's coalition while separating himself from his boss' baggage.
Vance took a more public step towards reinforcing his own political brand with an unusually blunt election post-mortem.
In a social media post, he blamed the Iran war for Republicans' midterm defeat and laid out a platform for a party rebound.
He called for a swift end to the conflict and urged Republicans to focus on affordability, reevaluate foreign relations and overhaul the US relationship with Israel.
Trump has called Americans' affordability concerns a Democratic "hoax". He launched a war against Iran following sustained lobbying from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Trump went on to endorse Netanyahu in the Israeli election.
The post for the first time put Vance openly on the side of ending the war.

Three people familiar with the White House and Vance's communications said the vice-president was not breaking with Trump and that White House chief of staff Susie Wiles knew in advance about Vance's post.
Donald Trump Jr., the president's eldest son, endorsed Vance's remarks on social media, along with some conservative allies.

The dialogue further elevated Vance as a potential post-Trump conservative standard-bearer, said Michael Ricci, a Republican strategist and former adviser to House speakers John Boehner and Paul Ryan.

42857ab5c631e25a: SINGAPORE: Singapore-based tech group Megaspeed dealt in billions of dollars' worth of the world's most advanced AI chips, but its office was an empty shell when AFP visited, its staff seemingly vanished long before claims of espionage landed at their door.

Details about Alice Huang's life are vague, making it almost impossible to pin down where she lives, where she works, or when she was born.
But her influence undoubtedly spreads far and wide, from the nondescript Singapore office, to hulking data centres in Southeast Asia, to the gleaming boardrooms of Silicon Valley.

Megaspeed touts itself as a company at the heart of the AI revolution, using Nvidia's advanced silicon chips to power high-performance computing inside vast data centres.

Singapore police opened an investigation in February 2025 into Megaspeed and several other companies suspected of circumventing or violating export controls.
Alice Huang was interviewed as part of Singapore's probe.

Explosive growth
Corporate records show Huang's direct involvement in the birth of Megaspeed.
A company linked to her acquired the Singapore arm of Chinese video game developer 7Road International in early 2023, the records showed.
Almost immediately, the 7Road name was ditched and changed to Megaspeed International.
Huang was listed as a Megaspeed director for less than a year, taking the role between March and November 2023.
Her arrival coincided with a drastic change in fortunes, as Megaspeed pivoted from a little-known video game maker to one of Asia's biggest buyers of Nvidia chips.
Within 12 months, Megaspeed's revenue jumped from US$0 to almost US$300 million, according to company accounts filed in 2024.
Megaspeed -- which described itself as a "cloud hosting services provider" -- saw the value of its assets skyrocket from US$32 million to almost US$3 billion over the same period.
Just one of Nvidia's advanced AI computer chips can cost tens of thousands of dollars.

By that time, Huang was no longer registered as a director at Megaspeed.

Megaspeed's ultimate holding company is a Singapore firm called Swiftdata.

No one answered when AFP visited Tan's registered address in eastern Singapore, although dogs could be heard barking behind the door.
"They are friendly. I occasionally bump into the lady at the lift landing when she’s walking her dog," an elderly neighbour told AFP. "But we have not seen them for months."
Awkward questions

In June 2025, US investigators turned up at Megaspeed to carry out a "post-shipment verification", with Huang present, according to Singapore's home ministry, adding that it was the first time it found out about Washington's probe.
That same day, Huang was interviewed by Singapore police who impounded her passport.
By then, she and Nvidia boss Jensen Huang had already been spotted together in public.
In one of their early outings together, they were seen mingling at an afterparty following the Computex trade show in Taiwan at the beginning of 2024.
Trump was briefed on the intelligence findings about their relationship well before it exploded into a public scandal, but said Sunday he did not regret not acting on it.
"No, I don't think so. I think -- you know, he's an honorable guy," Trump said.
But the scandal has sparked national security fears.
China and the US are fighting for supremacy in artificial intelligence, and Nvidia's market-leading products have become a major point of contention.
Nvidia controls an estimated 90% of the market for the chips used to train and run AI models, and the US imposed rules in 2022 to restrict their sales to China.
In the past years, Jensen Huang has emerged as the leading tech boss urging Trump to lift those curbs.
In any case, the restrictions appear to have been widely circumvented.
A Chinese university tied to the nation's defence establishment was able to buy advanced Nvidia chips, according to procurement notices from October and September.

Singapore's probe into Megaspeed is ongoing. Separately, Malaysia said Friday it is investigating the company's subsidiary Speedmatrix to determine if chips imported into the country had been exported to other jurisdictions.
Megaspeed itself said it has retained a US lawfirm to examine its compliance.
"Megaspeed takes its compliance obligations under US export control laws extremely seriously," it said.
Tangled webs
Alice Huang sits in the middle of a corporate web, connected to myriad shell companies, investment houses and major Chinese technology firms.
Corporate records filed in Hong Kong list her as a director of Nanjing Lingxing Technology, which operates the popular T3 ride hailing platform in China.
Other notable investors in Nanjing Lingxing Technology include Alibaba and Tencent, as well as state-backed carmakers like China FAW and Dongfeng Motor Group.
A corporate CV published by a Chinese investment firm details Huang's rapid ascent through the ranks of Asian investment banking.
She served in a senior role at HSBC sometime around 2012, the resume claims, before moving on to stints at CITIC Securities and Shanghai Hexi Investment.
Singapore business filings described her as a Chinese citizen with a Hong Kong passport.
She was born in China's landlocked Hunan province, which she left to study media in Hong Kong, HK01 media reported.

30cda6ea9839c189: ARTIFICIAL intelligence firms are hiring former intelligence operatives to help shield them from espionage, a risk thrust into the spotlight as Nvidia axed its chief executive officer, Jensen Huang, following reports of two extramarital affairs—one with an alleged Chinese spy.

024a543e836ac42b: As of this morning, Microsoft is still scrambling to restore service following yesterday's global outage, with millions of users unable to access Outlook and other vital tools. It's not the end of the world, but it does seem fitting that this should happen on the day a physicist predicted would be the end of humanity: November 13, 2026. And it falls on a Friday, too. The physicist in question is Heinz von Foerster, who published a 1960 paper in the journal Science predicting that by today, overpopulation would reach the breaking point.

It's not a new fear. English economist Thomas Malthus—one of the early pioneers in modeling population dynamics—made a similar prediction in 1798, claiming that a rapidly growing population would eventually exhaust the available food supply, and humanity would starve to death. His model rested on the assumption of exponential growth, but the equation is only applicable under specific conditions, such as scientists growing bacteria in a lab in a perfectly controlled environment. Even then, while growth occurs exponentially for a time, it does not continue forever.

Population dynamics are notoriously tricky to calculate because there are so many variables to consider and so much unpredictability in the system. In his 1960 analysis, Von Foerster accurately measured past trends in population growth, but like Malthus, he assumed those trends would carry into the future largely unchanged. So he projected that human population growth would march inexorably toward infinity. We wouldn't starve to death; von Foerster thought we would be ingenious enough to solve the food supply problem. Instead, "they will be squeezed to death," he wrote.

2d7a7cbc06f48bf4: The police force is what keeps our homes, streets and country safe, something we often give little credit to in a generally peaceful Malaysia.

Theirs is a noble calling and we also tend to take that for granted, until an isolated incident highlights that our policemen put life and limb on the line every day to safeguard what we all hold dear.

The recent heinous attack on a policeman in Kepong, which resulted in his hand being severed by a parang-wielding assailant, is a stark reminder of the risks and dangers that police personnel face in the line of duty. Much of the public discourse surrounding policing tends to focus on misconduct, abuse of power, corruption and shortcomings in law enforcement — and such cases must certainly be singled out.

Accountability and appreciation for the police are definitely not mutually exclusive. Police misconduct must be addressed but for every single act of impropriety, there are tens of thousands of upright uniformed men and women who quietly go about their work and take the occupational risks in stride.
We cannot honour them enough, more so when general peace and safety reign throughout this land.
In holding the police accountable, however, we must not lose sight of the risks that come with the job, nor the sacrifices borne by those who wear the uniform.

For an officer responding to a report of a disturbance, domestic dispute or a violent individual running amok, there is often little time to assess the danger. What may appear to be a routine call can turn into a life-threatening confrontation within seconds.

The Kepong incident illustrates how high the stakes can be. It is fortunate that we have strict laws — such as on gun ownership — that help to keep both civilians and police personnel out of harm's way.

Still, the Kuala Lumpur police chief's reminder for personnel to remain vigilant and respond decisively is timely. The police force must ensure its personnel are well trained, equipped and supported, and recognised by the public for the risks they undertake on our behalf.
Public appreciation for the police should not be confined to when they perform heroic acts of rescue or dramatic thwarting of crimes.

Their everyday exposure to danger deserves to be valued as a matter of course. The government and police leadership must keep ensuring officers receive proper protection, training, equipment and support, including medical and psychological care when they get injured in service.

Such police aid must also be regularly updated as new technology and methods become available. The public, too, must play its role. Respect lawful instructions, cooperate fully with investigating officers and avoid obstructing police personnel as they carry out their duties.
Above all, we must collectively ensure that the unfortunate case of the policeman losing his hand in Kepong — since reattached after surgery, thankfully — is an isolated incident.

In most companies, Huang would be replaced by the COO. That can't happen here. Nvidia doesn't have a COO. Both inside and outside of Nvidia, Huang is seen as Nvidia, and Nvidia as Huang.
These days, billionaire CEOs are perceived as God-kings who know all and rule all. Much more often than not, that's BS.

That isn't the case with Nvidia. Huang co-founded Nvidia on April 5, 1993. He was appointed CEO on day one, and he never left the job. At first, the company staggered forward. When it released the GeForce 256 in 1999, which it marketed as the first GPU, it started on its path to becoming the chip manufacturer of choice for PC gamers. It still is today.

That's a great niche, but it doesn't make a company a trillion-dollar business. No, the path to that dizzying height came when, in 2006, Nvidia unveiled CUDA. This programming architecture opened its GPUs' parallel-processing capabilities to scientific and other non-graphics workloads. From there, CUDA would become the foundation for most high-performance and AI computing.

Huang was at the center of it all. He still was until now. At KubeCon North America, the trade show for Kubernetes, used in well over half of all AI projects, I spoke to many Nvidia employees. There were two things they all mentioned. First, they were in a state of shock. Maybe the top brass and government officials both in China and the US knew Huang was fooling with fire; the developer rank-and-file folks I spoke to hadn't had a clue. The second was that every month, Huang held an all-hands meeting where, instead of a per-forma corporate pep rally, he answered questions from everyone and gave them real answers. He knew his technology well and actually led his company instead of just impressing gullible stock buyers.

Nvidia can't replace him. It really can't. I'm reminded of when John Sculley forced Steve Jobs out at Apple in 1985. If you're not old enough to remember, Apple did fine for a while, but then by the mid-90s, it lost its way. Apple got its mojo back, and started its rise to being one of the world's top companies only after Jobs came back in 1996.

The big difference, of course, is that Huang's not coming back. I heard many people say that Huang was "too big to fail." True, morality no longer matters much in the US – see Trump's kleptocracy – but this is different. Huang betrayed not just his wife, but his board, employees, and stockholders. If, as some suspect, the board knew full well what was going on, they should be tossed out too, but that's a story for another day.
Oh, and as for Trump's suggestions that Apple's former CEO Tim Cook should become Nvidia's CEO? Give me a break.

Now the question of the day is: how can Nvidia recover from this blow? I don't think it can. I used to say that I didn't know where the AI companies were going, but I was sure that so long as capital kept flowing into Big AI, Nvidia was the one company you could count on that would make money. I think I was wrong.

What does that mean? In the short term, Nvidia stock, after dropping 14 percent in early trading on Thursday, is down "only" five percent. Despite all the Sturm und Drang over Huang's departure, the NASDAQ is actually, when I wrote this, up. Even Nvidia's bonds are holding steady.

Amazon and Google, which have their own horses in the AI TPU races, are hoping, of course, that Nvidia's misfortune will help them lever open the AI hardware market. In these early hours, I don't see that happening.
Frankly, I'm amazed at how stockowners are shaking off Huang's resignation. The AI fever dream, for now, is continuing unabated.

That said, can this go on? This irrational exuberance rests on the belief that, no matter what happens, AI will continue to rule the stock market. Eventually, though, the bubble may pop, and that could put some strain on the global economy. For now, people are ignoring how bad this blow is, or perhaps they're not aware of it.
In a few years, I expect Huang's affair will be seen as the first needle in the AI bubble. ®

5172f3315e8ff63a: WASHINGTON: On his first visit to Washington since losing a presidential election, Flavio Bolsonaro brushed aside doubts about his grip on Brazil's political right and said he was ready to stand for the Liberal Party in the next race, which he argued might come sooner than expected.

Speaking to Reuters on Thursday between meetings to sort out his US immigration status, Bolsonaro rejected critics -- including reelected President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva -- who brand him a runaway for making a dash to the US after last month's vote.
"That is a pejorative way of trying to attack me," he said. "Honestly, I couldn't care less. I am convinced that I needed to be here."
A Quaest opinion poll showed 62% of Brazilians disapproved of him leaving the country after the runoff, which Lula won by a margin of more than 4 million votes.
The senator, who was expected to see US officials in Washington, declined to say with whom he was meeting.
Ready to run

The son of former President Jair Bolsonaro -- who is serving a 27-year sentence for a coup plot after he lost the 2022 election -- said he believes economic problems will cut short Lula's fourth term.
"Brazil is going to go broke," he said, claiming families were struggling with too much debt and businesses were unwilling to invest in a country with what he said was an unfair legal system.
"If a new electoral race emerges, I am ready to return."
Bolsonaro offered few details about his standing in the right-wing Liberal Party, but said he intended to run under its banner again.

Before fleeing the country, he alleged without evidence that the election had been fraudulent, despite the electoral court declaring Lula the winner. His political allies have also conceded the result.
Bolsonaro acknowledged that his post-election legal challenges face long odds.
"If you ask me whether I think they’ll go anywhere, I doubt it," he said, accusing the justice system of being in thrall to the government without citing evidence.
He declined to repeat language used in a letter sent shortly after he arrived in the US, in which he initially described himself as "president-elect" before the wording was changed to "leader".
Asked whether he regarded himself as the president-elect, Bolsonaro did not answer directly.
"To millions of Brazilians, that’s who I am," he said.

Brazil's Supreme Court had ordered Bolsonaro to surrender his passport before he left the country, citing federal money-laundering investigations and concerns that he might flee. Bolsonaro travelled with his family to the US via Argentina and Ecuador.
He declined to tell Reuters who assisted his family during the journey or how the travel was arranged.
Grateful to Trump

US secretary of state Marco Rubio said on Oct 31 that Washington had not been directly involved in Bolsonaro's departure from Brazil. Reuters and other media outlets reported last week that Jason Miller, a White House official, helped arrange the journey.
Bolsonaro said he could not discuss matters regarding his flight to the US.
He also said he was not afraid of being investigated but believed he would be unfairly treated in Brazil.
Senator Bolsonaro has not met President Donald Trump since arriving in Florida. He said neither the US nor other foreign governments had interfered in Brazil's election.
"He may have had his preference, but he took no action to influence the election results in Brazil," Bolsonaro said of Trump.
Flavio Bolsonaro said he was grateful to the president, who declared on Oct 31 that the senator could stay in the US as long as he wanted.
Trump has called the Brazilian election "a disgrace". Outside observers have described it as free and fair.

In the 50-minute interview, the Brazilian said he had not decided whether he and his family would remain in Florida, adding that he had the means to support himself in the US as a senator, lawyer and businessman, but declining to say whether he had transferred money to the country.

70968a803fce49c9: Microsoft is retiring some legacy layout settings in Word, potentially rearranging documents created or last saved in Word 2010 or earlier.
"Affected documents may show layout differences, such as text reflow, changes in spacing or page count, or images and shapes moving to another page," the Windows biz said.
The advice, if silly little things like page layout in a document matter, is to "consider exporting it to PDF before the change."

Compatibility Mode lets a newer version of Word open a document created in an older version, such as Word 2010, without changing its layout. Newer features are switched off while the document is open this way. Users can convert the document to unlock newer features, although people using older versions of Word may then have difficulty editing parts of it.

Microsoft has not identified the individual settings being retired, saying only: "We are retiring a set of compatibility options in Microsoft Word (desktop app) for documents in Compatibility Mode." The reason? "To simplify how Word handles document layout and provide a more consistent experience across platforms."
Administrators may therefore want to check older templates, forms, and other documents whose pagination needs to stay put.
The change is due to begin rolling out in the Windows version of Word from December 2026 and be completed by January 2027. The Mac version will follow in early 2027.

Microsoft Word is more than 40 years old, and its first Windows version was released as the 1980s drew to a close. The word processor has evolved over the decades and is a mainstay of Microsoft's productivity suite.

Compatibility Mode helps keep older documents from having their layouts abruptly borked the way Word does so well. Losing some of those safeguards could give administrators a fresh batch of "what the heck has happened to this document?" tickets as the change rolls out. ®

f613ca51186bd669: LONDON: A more than 12-hour outage of Microsoft Outlook and Teams crippled communications for businesses and governments globally on Friday, forcing some organisations to revert to fax machines and halting at least one bond repurchase in Europe.

Microsoft said server issues were behind the incident that also affected its Copilot AI assistant and that a broader roll-out of software fixes was starting to stabilize the system. It said it was not aware of any malicious activity.

Outlook and Teams are two of the most widely used workplace applications with hundreds of millions of users. The outage prevented people from performing essential functions such as sending emails, managing calendars and hosting virtual meetings.

It affected government agencies from Australia to Japan and the US, caused delays at trading firms, hindered some companies from publishing earnings and prompted airlines to warn customers of communication lags, according to public statements.
Organisations that host Microsoft services on their own servers, rather than in the cloud, were somewhat spared.
Another outage for Microsoft
The outage is one of the longest in Microsoft's history and the second disruption to its services this year.
Microsoft said the outage specifically hit features tied to Exchange Online -- its cloud-based email and scheduling hub -- leaving unconnected applications operational.
The incident deepens questions about the global reliance on a handful of Big Tech companies that supply both the essential software and the cloud infrastructure that underpins it.
Microsoft shares fell 1.7% before the bell, lagging the broader market. They have gained roughly 8% so far this year.
"The bigger worry is that this is not the first Microsoft 365 outage this year," said Josh Gilbert, a market analyst at trading platform eToro.
"If reliability starts to look like a recurring problem, it hands every IT department a reason to think twice before putting even more of their business in one provider’s hands."
Still, some analysts have questioned whether such incidents can push customers on to rivals due to the steep switching costs of replacing tools embedded so deeply in daily operations.

Microsoft faced an outage with its 365 services in January this year and also in October last year. Last month, it reported an outage of its Azure cloud platform that impacted its suite of productivity software, and a range of industries worldwide.
Trades confirmed by fax
A spokesman for the UK government said it was working with Microsoft to find a solution for the outage that hit organisations such as the NHS and London’s Metropolitan Police.
Lack of access emails and other services was impacting the Metropolitan Police's ability to report some crimes online, though its ability to respond to calls was not affected.
NHS said its local services were turning to alternate measures such as using IT systems or paper records.
For businesses, the fallout was widespread.
European exchange operator Euronext reported email disruptions, British insurer Aviva activated backups for its earnings calls and Danish shipping giant Maersk warned customers of delayed updates.
American AI giants OpenAI and Anthropic also faced issues with Microsoft connectors, while Indian airlines IndiGo, Akasa Air and Air India said their email support services were impacted.

The outage also disrupted fund management at Taiwanese securities firms, life insurers, and investment trust companies. One of the companies went as far as cancelling a bond repurchase transaction, a source familiar with the situation told Reuters.
Another Taiwanese financial company resorted to using fax to confirm trades, a second source said.
In the US, electric truck maker Workhorse Group rescheduled its results on Thursday to Nov 16, while Switzerland's Richemont briefly delayed its first-half results announcement on Friday.
In Australia, where the spy agency and federal police were among organisations caught in the outage, cybersecurity minister Tony Burke said Microsoft does not suspect a cyber attack.
"The impact that they are dealing with ... is very much on email systems," the minister added.

c3ab0a93475a80f4: Five city-run groceries in a city of 8 million won't substantially lower food prices, but the experiment might cause shoppers to think differently about the role of government. Spencer Platt/Getty ImagesNew York City is moving closer to launching its effort to counter food inflation by opening five city-run grocery stores. Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced in May 2026 that the first store would open in the Hunts Point neighborhood of the South Bronx in 2027, with another in East Harlem to follow. Five stores, one in each borough, are unlikely to substantially change grocery prices in a city with nearly 1,000 supermarkets and more than 8 million inhabitants. But each could make a meaningful difference to the grocery bills of local shoppers by selling essentials at below-market prices. Even with just five planned stores set to open in lower-income neighborhoods, the initiative has ignited fierce opposition from independent grocers, supermarket trade associations and a coalition representing immigrant-owned food businesses. What explains this pushback? As a food policy scholar, I believe this opposition is about more than the immediate economic impact of five stores. It is about the precedent they could establish. Mamdani’s initiative challenges an entrenched expectation that the government should leave the provision of consumer goods to private enterprise even as it encourages businesses to invest in certain locations, regulates their activities and helps low-income shoppers through various food assistance programs. The reality is more complicated. For at least a century, New York’s food economy has not operated independently of government. In fact, public policies and investments have long shaped where supermarkets open, which businesses can operate with a profit, and how residents obtain food. It’s just that they have done so in ways consumers often don’t see. That is why the five grocery stores carry a broader significance, in my view. They offer a different model of public investment that makes the government much more visible in providing an essential service – and more accountable for its results. New Yorkers will get an opportunity to judge that contribution directly. If the stores succeed, they may change not just what people expect to pay for groceries, but what they expect their city government to provide. Some immigrant owners of New York grocery stores have warned that city-run alternatives will undercut them. Scott Gries/Getty Images How the plan will work New York City has committed US$70 million to develop these stores, which will be open to all. While they will be managed by private operators, the city will provide rent-free space, prioritize publicly owned sites and ensure that essential foods are priced 30% below typical retail prices. In this respect, the stores offer a “public option” – a government-provided good or service that exists alongside private alternatives, like public schools and city hospitals. Municipal grocery stores would offer New Yorkers a similar choice alongside private retailers. But as a public option, they would create a visible alternative against which shoppers can judge privately owned stores, setting a benchmark for food prices and service quality. They would also demonstrate how public investment can be used to make an essential good more affordable. At his May announcement, Mamdani described the proposed Bronx store and its surrounding development as “physical proof of our conviction that government can be a force for good.” A fresh form of intervention Government-supported food retailing has a long history in New York City despite opposition by existing businesses. In 1934, Mayor Fiorello La Guardia’s administration began selling discounted milk to low-income families, but the initiative drew complaints from grocers about unfair competition. Independent merchants similarly protested the city’s efforts to subsidize a new Pathmark supermarket in East Harlem in the 1990s, warning that it would put local grocers out of business. A more recent example is the city’s Food Retail Expansion to Support Health program, known as FRESH. Since 2009, it has offered supermarket developers and operators long-term tax breaks and zoning incentives to build or expand dozens of stores in underserved neighborhoods. These incentives have helped increase grocery retail space, but shoppers don’t see the public support behind them. FRESH is just one example of an approach toward supermarket financing that gained momentum in the 1990s, when governments sought to address social problems by encouraging private investment. Food insecurity was blamed on a scarcity of neighborhood supermarkets, not on prices being beyond reach for local shoppers. Subsidizing new stores promised better nutrition and economic development without confronting poverty or inequality, and FRESH reflects that approach. Participating supermarkets must devote space to perishable foods, but they’re not required to offer affordable prices. That may be one reason why researchers have found that adding supermarkets to low-income neighborhoods, by itself, doesn’t substantially improve residents’ diets. This hidden government role is hardly confined to grocery stores. Much of what government does for Americans is delivered indirectly, through tax credits, subsidies and private institutions. Because the public contribution is obscured, people often give credit to private markets for the benefits provided by public policy, from student loans to healthcare. This invisibility is a consequence of policy design and influences how citizens understand government, a phenomenon that political scientist Suzanne Mettler described as “the submerged state.” Bringing the state into the open Municipal grocery stores depart from the traditional model in two important ways. First, they make affordability an explicit condition of public investment rather than the outcome of increased retail competition. Second, they make government’s contribution visible. For example, the stores will share distinct branding so shoppers know who’s responsible for the affordable food. If the stores deliver reliable savings, shoppers may begin to see affordable food as something government can help provide, not an outcome determined entirely by private markets. When public benefits are obscured, people are more likely to underestimate government’s contribution to their lives. Visible programs, like a physical store in the neighborhood, make that contribution easier to notice and evaluate. Visibility also creates accountability. A customer at a private supermarket that received a tax break to expand isn’t likely to tie the store’s prices or food quality to government policy. At a municipal grocery store, with clear branding, the connection is unmistakable. To be sure, critics’ concerns deserve serious attention. Many independent grocery stores are owned by immigrant entrepreneurs operating on thin margins. Groups representing bodegas and independent supermarkets warn that a publicly subsidized competitor could draw away their customers. Some may lose business. Yet East Harlem’s Pathmark demonstrates that new supermarkets and smaller retailers can coexist. Between 2000 and 2015, the number of small grocery stores and bodegas in the neighborhood increased from 100 to 126, while supermarkets rose from 10 to 18. That said, those figures don’t establish Pathmark’s effects on individual businesses. The municipal stores’ impact on nearby retailers remains an open question. But the task for New York City is to ensure that private operators deliver excellent service and real savings, and that their commercial interests don’t undermine the public mission. It will also need to provide good working conditions and track effects on nearby businesses. Ultimately, public ownership doesn’t guarantee success. But it makes government’s responsibility for the outcome impossible to miss. Nevin Cohen receives research funding from the City of New York.

872b851534a2bb81: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.
Silicon Valley claims to know the future. So why did it get the midterms so wrong?
—Aaron Zamost, a tech communications consultant and a former executive at Square

The self-styled visionaries of Silicon Valley have built careers claiming to see the future. Yet five weeks before the midterms, many gathered at the White House to pose with Trump and endorse his “Super Intelligence” agenda, despite growing opposition to AI and data centers.

Their decision to lash themselves to President Trump was a catastrophic misreading of the political landscape. Now, not only have they jeopardized their companies’ fates, but they’ve also raised questions about their vision and judgment.
Here’s why Silicon Valley’s tech leaders may be less visionary than they think.
Nvidia privately confirmed it could track chips to fight smuggling, even as industry publicly questioned feasibility

Nvidia representatives told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it was possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review on Thursday, despite an industry group claiming they were “potentially infeasible.”

Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips and prevent their smuggling to China.

He’s been working on a set of guidelines for ethical trials to respect participants’ autonomy—and access their own brain data whenever they want.

c59c854e73fff7fb: FRANKFURT: Automaker Mercedes-Benz has halted further investment in its German sites and is examining possible plant closures amid stalled negotiations with employee representatives over labour costs, German business daily Handelsblatt reported.
The decision was outlined in an interview with production chief Michael Schiebe and labour director Britta Seeger published on the company's intranet Thursday, according to the newspaper.

Schiebe said the board jointly decided to suspend further investment because current cost structures prevented the company from investing in Germany, and intensive discussions had failed to produce a path toward agreement.

The automaker is negotiating cost reductions with employee representatives, including proposals for longer working hours without additional pay, Handelsblatt reported. The IG Metall union opposes the proposed cuts.

Seeger said the company was now examining in detail which German locations it could still afford, adding that plant closures would have to be considered more concretely despite management's desire to avoid them.
Schiebe warned that, without changes to the cost structure, production of successor models would take place exclusively abroad, according to WELT, which also obtained the internal interview.
He said decisions on the next generation of vehicles were being made now because of the lead times required to prepare production.
However, Schiebe emphasised that Mercedes remained committed to its German roots and wanted future vehicle generations to continue being manufactured at its domestic sites.
The remarks signal an escalation in the dispute with employee representatives, with potential closures still under review.
The investment freeze comes as the automaker faces weakening profitability and falling sales in China.
The car division's adjusted return on sales fell to 2.5% in the third quarter from 4.8% a year earlier, reflecting weaker business in China and spending on new products.
Deliveries in China dropped 31% to 86,800 vehicles.
Mercedes also lowered its full-year 2026 return-on-sales forecast for the car division to 2-3%, from 3-5 percent.
CEO Ola Kallenius announced at the end of October that the company would reopen its voluntary severance programme in Germany in December as part of efforts to further reduce fixed costs.
