ddfa9f9164d4ad73: SINGAPORE, Nov 13 — Singapore-based tech group Megaspeed dealt in billions of dollars’ worth of the world’s most advanced AI chips, but its office was an empty shell when AFP visited, its staff seemingly vanished long before claims of espionage landed at their door.
Megaspeed’s former director Alice Huang was this week outed as an alleged Chinese spy, accused of having an affair with Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang while digging up company secrets for Beijing.
Details about Alice Huang’s life are vague, making it almost impossible to pin down where she lives, where she works, or when she was born.
But her influence undoubtedly spreads far and wide, from the nondescript Singapore office, to hulking data centres in South-east Asia, to the gleaming boardrooms of Silicon Valley.
Her connection to cloud computing firm Megaspeed sits at the centre of the scandal.
Megaspeed touts itself as a company at the heart of the AI revolution, using Nvidia’s advanced silicon chips to power high-performance computing inside vast data centres.
But it is also under investigation for serving a murkier purpose.
Under the guise of buying computer hardware for its South-east Asia data hubs, Megaspeed has allegedly helped Beijing skirt trade restrictions by sending Nvidia chips into China.
Beijing has denied allegations of spying, and Megaspeed said it was investigating if it had complied with export controls on the sensitive chips.
At Megaspeed’s office in the heart of the Singapore business district, no staff could be seen behind its locked glass doors.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
The office of Megaspeed International at the Ocean Financial Centre building in Singapore as seen on November 10, 2026. — AFP pic
Neighbours told AFP they had not seen anyone come or go for the past few months.
Likewise in a mall at a newly developed neighbourhood in Johor, the Malaysian region a bridge away from Singapore, no employees were around in subsidiary Speedmatrix’s office.
Singapore police opened an investigation in February 2025 into Megaspeed and several other companies suspected of circumventing or violating export controls.
Alice Huang was interviewed as part of Singapore’s probe.
Although no charges were laid, she was barred from the city-state in February 2026 for providing inaccurate information to “downplay her role in Megaspeed”, Singapore’s home ministry said.
Explosive growth
Corporate records show Huang’s direct involvement in the birth of Megaspeed.
A company linked to her acquired the Singapore arm of Chinese video game developer 7Road International in early 2023, the records showed.
Almost immediately, the 7Road name was ditched and changed to Megaspeed International.
Huang was listed as a Megaspeed director for less than a year, taking the role between March and November 2023.
Her arrival coincided with a drastic change in fortunes, as Megaspeed pivoted from a little-known video game maker to one of Asia’s biggest buyers of Nvidia chips.
Within 12 months, Megaspeed’s revenue jumped from zero to almost US$300 million (RM1.23 billion), according to company accounts filed in 2024.

Megaspeed – which described itself as a “cloud hosting services provider” – saw the value of its assets skyrocket from US$32 million (RM131 million) to almost US$3 billion (RM12.3 billion) over the same period.
Just one of Nvidia’s advanced AI computer chips can cost tens of thousands of dollars.
Over two years, Megaspeed reportedly traded in upwards of US$4 billion (RM16.4 billion) worth of Nvidia chips.
A financial trail weaving through Singapore, Malaysia and the Cayman Islands suggests Megaspeed’s business may have been boosted by a connection to Chinese tech giant Alibaba.
Megaspeed has a Malaysian subsidiary that struck a deal in 2024 pledging assets to Apex Enterprise Solutions in Singapore as security in case of contractual breaches.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
The office of Speedmatrix, a Megaspeed subsidiary under investigation in Malaysia, at an office in Eco Botanic township in Johor on November 13, 2026. — AFP pic
Apex is linked through a parent company to Alibaba Group Holding Ltd, a firm registered in the Cayman Islands, Singapore corporate data shows.
By that time, Huang was no longer registered as a director at Megaspeed.
But Singapore authorities said she remained one of Megaspeed’s “key controllers”.
Megaspeed’s ultimate holding company is a Singapore firm called Swiftdata.
Singapore businessman Tan Yong Pong – who has previously run printing and graphic design companies – is a director of both Megaspeed and Swiftdata.
No one answered when AFP visited Tan’s registered address in eastern Singapore, although dogs could be heard barking behind the door.
“They are friendly.
“I occasionally bump into the lady at the lift landing when she’s walking her dog,” an elderly neighbour told AFP.
“But we have not seen them for months.”
Awkward questions

In June 2025, US investigators turned up at Megaspeed to carry out a “post-shipment verification”, with Huang present, according to Singapore’s home ministry, adding that it was the first time it found out about Washington’s probe.
That same day, Huang was interviewed by Singapore police who impounded her passport.
By then, she and Nvidia boss Jensen Huang had already been spotted together in public.
In one of their early outings together, they were seen mingling at an afterparty following the Computex trade show in Taiwan at the beginning of 2024.
Trump was briefed on the intelligence findings about their relationship well before it exploded into a public scandal, but said Sunday he did not regret not acting on it.
“No, I don’t think so.
“I think – you know, he’s an honorable guy,” Trump said.
But the scandal has sparked national security fears.
China and the United States are fighting for supremacy in artificial intelligence, and Nvidia’s market-leading products have become a major point of contention.
Nvidia controls an estimated 90 per cent of the market for the chips used to train and run AI models, and the US imposed rules in 2022 to restrict their sales to China.
In the past years, Jensen Huang has emerged as the leading tech boss urging Trump to lift those curbs.
In any case, the restrictions appear to have been widely circumvented.
A Chinese university tied to the nation’s defence establishment was able to buy advanced Nvidia chips, according to procurement notices from October and September.
Singapore’s probe into Megaspeed is ongoing.
Separately, Malaysia said Friday it is investigating the company’s subsidiary Speedmatrix to determine if chips imported into the country had been exported to other jurisdictions.
Megaspeed itself said it has retained a US law firm to examine its compliance.
“Megaspeed takes its compliance obligations under US export control laws extremely seriously,” it said.
Tangled webs
Alice Huang sits in the middle of a corporate web, connected to myriad shell companies, investment houses and major Chinese technology firms.
Corporate records filed in Hong Kong list her as a director of Nanjing Lingxing Technology, which operates the popular T3 ride hailing platform in China.
Other notable investors in Nanjing Lingxing Technology include Alibaba and Tencent, as well as state-backed carmakers like China FAW and Dongfeng Motor Group.
A corporate CV published by a Chinese investment firm details Huang’s rapid ascent through the ranks of Asian investment banking.
She served in a senior role at HSBC sometime around 2012, the resume claims, before moving on to stints at CITIC Securities and Shanghai Hexi Investment.
Singapore business filings described her as a Chinese citizen with a Hong Kong passport.
She was born in China’s landlocked Hunan province, which she left to study media in Hong Kong, HK01 media reported.
A CCTV reporter wrote on Weibo that she worked with Huang at the Chinese broadcaster, but later deleted the post. — AFP
129864770b7eeebd: TAIPEI, Nov 13 — Taiwan-born Jensen Huang, the former boss of Nvidia, was feted like a rock star on visits to his birthplace, posing for selfies with fans and being mobbed by journalists.
His spectacular downfall might change that.

Huang’s once “flawless” image in Taiwan has been shattered by revelations of two extramarital affairs – including one with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy – that forced him to resign from the company he founded.
“I thought he had the persona of a devoted husband, and it turns out he’s kind of a scumbag,” Ivan Liang, 28, told AFP during his lunch break on Friday.
Huang has been a source of pride and inspiration for many Taiwanese.
While other tech titans kept a low profile, Huang was chatty and charming in public, readily signing autographs and posing for photos.
“I definitely think my perception of him has changed because, after all, he originally had that ‘nation’s dad’ image,” said Leo Fu, a 42-year-old import distributor.
“I feel like that image of him has probably taken a hit in the eyes of the general public in Taiwan.”
Dessert shop owner Jane Hsieh, 70, still has fond memories of Huang visiting her store on multiple occasions for one of her traditional tofu puddings.

“Before this, he felt like such a flawless person,” Hsieh told AFP in her shop where photos of her and her husband posing with the leather-jacketed Huang, his wife Lori, and son Spencer, are proudly displayed.
“It’s just a shame because he gave everyone the impression that he was a really great guy, and he was always very polite when he came here,” she said.
While her feelings about Huang have changed as a result of the affairs, Hsieh said she would not remove the photos from her shop.
“Why kick someone when they’re down?” she said.
Pretty outrageous

At the Chinese restaurant where one of Huang’s lovers – identified as suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang – was filmed kissing him on the cheek in May 2025, a plate signed by Huang on the same night is still on display.
Staff were reluctant to talk about the infamous evening to AFP on Friday, only saying they were always focused on serving their customers.
“I think it’s pretty outrageous,” 38-year-old Chen Yu-ting, who works in finance, said of Huang’s affair with someone believed to have spied for Beijing.
“If the other person really was trying to use him, it seems like he was just way too easily deceived,” she said.
“Given his status, he really should be paying much closer attention to the people around him and who he associates with.”
While Huang’s affairs have tarnished his reputation, some Taiwanese are more concerned about the impact the scandal could have on Taiwan’s economy and stock market.
Huang has generated huge amounts of wealth for the island at the centre of the global artificial intelligence (AI) technology boom.
Nvidia’s advanced chips critical to the AI buildout are made by Taiwanese tech titan TSMC and have helped drive Taiwan’s stocks to record highs and push its economy into double-digit growth.
Ivan Liang, who works in imports and exports, said he was “very worried”.
“The market crashed... a few days ago, and then Nvidia’s stock price just kept dropping and dropping and dropping,” Liang said.
“I don’t trade US stocks myself, but the US and Taiwan stock markets definitely move in tandem and affect each other,” he said.
“Whatever he does is none of my business – I only care about my money.” — AFP
9c438f9b504b40fe: SAN FRANCISCO, Nov 13 — Hours after Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia, shocked tech insiders at a conference in San Francisco saw his departure as troubling for the business but were uncertain over how heavy the impact would be.

Many were still processing the spectacular departure of the rockstar CEO, who came to embody the global boom for AI chips but fell from grace after revelations of multiple extramarital affairs, one reportedly with a Chinese spy.
“It’s a blow to I think everything and pretty much every player in (the) space, except direct competitors,” Databricks CEO Ali Ghodsi said in onstage remarks.
“The culture of the company is a lot... the personality of the CEO that is there for a long time,” Ghodsi said.
A lot now “depends on who the next CEO is,” he added.
Nvidia’s board has appointed Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress to replace Huang on an interim basis, but it remains unclear who will take over in the long term.
Investors had begun taking a dimmer view of the company even before news of the scandal broke.
Nvidia’s shares have lost 13 per cent of their value since Monday, and are down more than 26 per cent over the past month.
One venture capitalist told AFP that the fallout from Huang’s infidelities was accelerating a correction that had already been underway.
Show must go on
Others were more sanguine about the industry’s prospects.
“We’re very sad to see Jensen go,” Asher Spector, the founder of an artificial intelligence startup called Flapping Airplanes, said onstage at the Cerebral Valley AI Summit.
“That said, Nvidia has been a great partner,” Spector said, adding: “We’re very optimistic.”
A lighthearted note came from an arcade game in the style of “Mortal Kombat”, which pitted tech CEOs like Huang, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and even disgraced
Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes against each other.
Other major tech companies, including Microsoft, Uber and Apple, have survived and even thrived after the departure of era-defining executives.
Still, some attendees noted that Huang’s downfall might leave competing AI chip designers circling for a chance to grab a piece of Nvidia’s market share.
“It was kind of unimaginable to us that there would be a world where Nvidia wouldn’t be the biggest player a few years from now,” Robert Wachen, the co-founder of AI computing startup Etched, said.
“But now you see there’s probably a pretty big opening” for other players in the sector, Wachen said.
Open-model guru
Huang’s exit has particularly rattled the open software community.
The former Nvidia chief advocated for an ecosystem that includes so-called open models, which users can download and customise to varying degrees.
That differs from leading model developers like OpenAI, which makes ChatGPT, and Anthropic, which crafts Claude, both of which push for closed models.
Huang was “the leader of the pack” for open models and his departure does “create a lot of uncertainty,” Igor Babuschkin, the CEO of a startup called River AI, said.

He also led Nvidia to provide billions in financing commitments to other companies, notably a more than US$100 billion (RM409 billion) data centre for OpenAI, which sparked concerns about circular dealmaking and a growing tech bubble.
“Will circular deals face greater scrutiny and a reality check? Very likely,” Hivemind Capital partner Emmanuel Vallod told AFP via email.
“But does that mean the music is about to stop? I very much doubt it.” — AFP
e2cfcb5316f19f4c: OSLO, Nov 13 — Norway’s Supreme Court on Friday ruled that three oil licences granted by the government in the North Sea were invalid since their emissions impact had not adequately been accounted for.

The court agreed with climate campaigners, who challenged the validity of the licences, arguing that the environmental impact assessments had not considered the emissions from burning the oil after it had been extracted.
The campaigners had already won victories in two lower-court rulings.
The high court ruled that the plans for extraction and expansion were “invalid due to procedural errors”.
It noted that while emissions assessments were carried out, they only covered so-called production emissions and not the subsequent “combustion emissions”.
According to the court, “the combustion emissions resulting from petroleum production must be subject to an impact assessment” before a plan is approved.
For the highly anticipated decision, the court sat in plenary formation, meaning that 11 judges took part instead of the usual five – a format reserved for important cases.
Operations were allowed to continue at the three contested North Sea fields while the energy ministry appealed the rulings.
Norway’s Supreme Court in Oslo, where it ruled on November 13, 2026 in a climate lawsuit over North Sea oil licences. — AFP pic
The Supreme Court noted that the oil companies were not parties in the case and said the fact the approvals had been declared invalid did not automatically mean the licences ceased to apply.
“The ministry must, however, reassess the case on the basis of proper procedure,” the court said in a statement.

The ruling will be closely watched beyond the borders of the Scandinavian country by the many legal experts and environmental groups that have challenged production licences granted to oil companies on climate grounds. — AFP
1aea23c8cb0039c8: ROME, Nov 13 — “Luxury is the opposite of the naturally necessary,” wrote Karl Marx – but tell that to guests at a new five-star Rome hotel in the former seat of the Italian Communist Party (PCI).
For decades the headquarters of the biggest Communist party in the West, the imposing building just a few steps from Piazza Venezia in the city centre is now the Thompson Rome by Hyatt.
Its prices are not aimed at the proletariat: rooms range from €550 to €4,000 (RM2,585 to RM18,800) for a suite in high season.
And that makes it just the latest in a wave of five-star hotels opening in the European capital that has some locals looking askance.
“Who could have ever imagined it would end like this?” wrote La Repubblica newspaper at the hotel’s soft opening earlier this month, noting that Italy’s Communists were known as a “spartan lot”.
From the airy new lobby with travertine and marble elements, to its luxury rooms, little remains of the former headquarters.

It was here on June 21, 1976, that the party’s secretary-general, Enrico Berlinguer, stepped out on his office balcony to celebrate the 34.4 per cent of the vote won by the PCI, its best-ever showing.
“One out of three Italians votes Communist!” Berlinguer proclaimed to the ebullient crowd in the street below.
But the glory years did not last and the building was eventually sold by the debt-ridden successor party to the PCI, the Democrats of the Left (DS), in 2000.
Soon after, it was acquired by real estate and finance group Finanziaria Tosinvest, controlled by Antonio Angelucci, a deputy with the far-right League party.
Moving toward modernity
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

A room at the Thompson Rome by Hyatt that can cost anywhere between €550 and €4,000 (RM2,585–RM18,800) and which once served as the office of the Italian Communist Party’s secretary-general, in central Rome on November 11, 2026. — AFP pic
Construction on the original building first began in 1941, after the east-west artery Via delle Botteghe Oscure was widened, but work was interrupted by World War II.
That means it was conceived under Fascism and completed in its aftermath, said architect Renzo Costa, who led the building’s most recent renovation.
“This gives it that transformative significance, the opportunity to become a symbol, to change over time and then turn into a place of future political thought,” Costa told AFP.
“So this is a building that was born with the intention of moving toward modernity.”
Gazing over the entryway is a 1952 bronze bust of Antonio Gramsci – Italy’s most celebrated Marxist who helped found the party before dying in prison in 1937 under Mussolini.
Originally designed by Italian sculptor Gio Pomodoro, the entrance still boasts his stone relief sculpture covering an entire wall, with a hammer and sickle and Paris Commune sign.

The open, almost raw space retains a vintage feel, with 1940s-era armchairs, brass and glass sconces, and a bronze welcome desk whose pointed edges echo the large star incorporated into Pomodoro’s stone floor.
But you will find no mention of the building’s past on the hotel’s webpage.
Italians tend to know the building’s history and are curious, said hotel manager Arturo Reguero Gomez.
Other visitors, not so much.
“They need to know Italian history a bit better,” he laughed.
Place of capitalism
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Architect Renzo Costa, who led the transformation of the former Italian Communist Party headquarters into the Thompson Rome by Hyatt, poses on the hotel’s rooftop in central Rome on November 11, 2026. — AFP pic
As well as the PCI, the parties that dominated Italian politics last century – the Christian Democrats and the Italian Socialist Party – all occupied nearby buildings in the heart of Rome.

“They were powerful machines that kept the system running, with many officials; they needed to occupy buildings,” said ex-PCI member Claudio Velardi, chief of staff in the late 1990s to Massimo D’Alema, Italy’s only former Communist prime minister.
Ugo Sposetti, a former PCI senator and DS treasurer, said at one time about 360 people worked at the headquarters.
They included medical staff and 40 people as security and drivers.
Berlinguer had two armoured vehicles, he said.
But twenty years ago, the area had already transformed into a “place of capitalism”, with the arrival of multinational corporations and other firms, Velardi said.
Some are not pleased by the new opening.
A group of activists briefly burst into the lobby this week, calling for more low-cost housing instead of private hotels in Rome.
But architect Costa defended the transformation.
“This building was an abandoned building.
“Today it provides jobs for about a hundred people... So we carried out a restoration that respected its pre-existing state,” he said.
“We didn’t come in here, gut everything and turn it into, I don’t know, a supermarket, right?” — AFP
682046f465b6269a: TOKYO: Japan coach Hajime Moriyasu will step down next week, the country's football association said Friday, cutting short his tenure in the wake of the 2027 Asian Cup's postponement.
Moriyasu, Japan's longest-serving coach, was originally set to lead the team at the Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia in January before handing the reins to current Under-23 boss Go Oiwa.

But the Asian Football Confederation announced last week that the tournament would be pushed back to December 2027 due to "exceptional circumstances" in the region, following Houthi attacks on the host country.
That left Moriyasu in limbo, with Japan Football Association (JFA) chiefs last week declining to clarify when the coaching handover would take place.
They said on Friday that Japan's friendlies in Singapore against Brazil on Saturday and Paraguay on Tuesday would be Moriyasu's last in charge.
The 58-year-old took over after the 2018 World Cup.
He led Japan to shock wins over Germany and Spain on the way to a last-16 defeat on penalties to Croatia at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar.
He took them to the last 32 at this year's World Cup in North America, where they lost 2-1 to Brazil after a last-minute goal.
Moriyasu was set to lead the team in an Asian Cup warm-up friendly against a yet-to-be-named opponent in Osaka on December 30.
The JFA said that the game had been cancelled.
"We had regarded this game as an important opportunity to strengthen the Japan team and we had been making thorough preparations," JFA president Tsuneyasu Miyamoto said in a statement.
"But following the postponement of the Asian Cup and considering the national team's schedule, we have decided to cancel the game." - AFP
26aa455fdd109dee: ALOR GAJAH: Having been on the move since 9am, Barisan Nasional incumbent for Machap Jaya Datuk Ngwe Hee Sem is showing no signs of slowing down as campaigning enters its final hours ahead of tomorrow's polls.
With less than three hours before the campaign period ends, Ngwe is making a final push to reach as many constituents as possible.
He said his packed schedule was crucial to ensuring voters, including those who had returned from working elsewhere, were informed of his service record over the past five years.
"My schedule today is packed because I want to engage with as many voters as possible in Machap Jaya during these final hours before tonight's campaign deadline.

"Tonight is very important for me to explain to voters, especially young people returning from places such as Singapore and Kuala Lumpur, what I have accomplished as their elected representative over the past five years," he said.

Asked why constituents should retain him as their assemblyman, Ngwe cited his efforts to resolve a 30-year-old land dispute involving the former railway reserve in Melaka Pindah, which spans the Machap, Durian Tunggal, Rembia and Gadek state constituencies.
He also highlighted his efforts to safeguard the welfare and religious sensitivities of the Indian community by resolving two temple land issues in his constituency.
These included acquiring land within a private estate for a temple site to be gazetted. Indian voters make up 13.7 per cent of the electorate in Machap Jaya.
"As the assemblyman, I sought solutions through formal applications and land acquisition to secure proper temple land," he said.
"In Melaka, we do not take the approach seen in Selangor, where hundreds of temples were declared illegal," he added.

Ngwe said upgrading basic infrastructure in rural parts of Machap Jaya had remained a priority throughout his term. He cited the construction of new community halls and the installation of more than 100 solar-powered streetlights to improve visibility and safety at night.

e39943648c39dc83: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 13 — Several PKR leaders have criticised PAS president Tan Sri Abdul Hadi Awang over his remarks comparing Muslim and non-Muslim leaders, warning that religious sentiments should not be used to divide Malaysians for political gain.
PKR vice-president Datuk Chang Lih Kang said political differences should be debated based on policies and solutions to people’s problems rather than religious sentiments.

He described Abdul Hadi’s remarks during a Melaka state election campaign event yesterday as deeply disappointing, saying statements that hurt religious sensitivities and fuel tensions would only harm the country.
Abdul Hadi was quoted as saying that even the worst Muslim leaders governing a country would not be as oppressive as non-Muslims.

“As a religious figure with extensive knowledge, he should set an example in promoting good character and unity. Unfortunately, that knowledge is not reflected in the wisdom of his words,” Chang said in a statement today.
Chang, who is also Science, Technology and Innovation Minister, said Malaysia’s multiracial and multireligious harmony was essential to economic development, investor confidence and job creation.

He questioned whether the pursuit of political power should come at the expense of national unity and stability, stressing that Malaysia needed leaders who brought people together rather than divided them.

Meanwhile, PKR secretary-general Datuk Dr Fuziah Salleh questioned how Abdul Hadi’s remarks aligned with opposition political cooperation in Melaka, particularly involving MCA and Gerakan in the campaign for Kelebang seat.

“Interestingly, the MCA president had spoken at the same campaign event, while Gerakan president Dominic Lau also appealed to Barisan Nasional and Perikatan Nasional supporters to back a non-Muslim Gerakan candidate.

“This happened in front of a Malay-majority audience. So, how should Abdul Hadi’s remarks be interpreted in the context of their political cooperation?” said Fuziah, who is also Deputy Domestic Trade and Cost of Living Minister.

Fuziah also expressed support for Pakatan Harapan’s candidate for Kelebang, Farzana Hayani, saying that her links to the federal ruling coalition could help bring local concerns to the government’s attention regardless of race or religion.
Separately, PKR Youth (AMK) chief Muhammad Kamil Abdul Munim described Abdul Hadi’s remarks as extreme and prejudiced, warning that they could fuel religious hostility and undermine national unity.

He noted that it is all the more concerning that such a statement came from a senior political leader who possesses a background in religious education and wields significant influence within the Muslim community.

“Such a position and level of knowledge should be used to foster an understanding of Islam rooted in justice, wisdom, and noble character, not to cultivate the perception that a Muslim possesses an absolute moral superiority over followers of other religions, even when committing acts of injustice,” he said in a statement.

He said that the AMK views the attempt to weigh the severity of an injustice based on religious identity as a departure from the principle of justice, a fundamental tenet of Islamic teachings. Furthermore, it raises questions regarding the party’s sincerity in building political cooperation across racial and religious lines.

“Do such views also apply to the leaders of the MCA and Gerakan, who are PAS’s political partners? Or is this principle applied only when dealing with those who hold opposing political stances?” he asked.
As such, Muhammad Kamil urged Abdul Hadi to publicly clarify and retract his remarks, saying justice should apply equally regardless of race, religion or political affiliation.
He stressed that Malaysia’s future must be grounded in constitutional principles, respect for Islam as the religion of the Federation and the protection of religious freedom for all citizens.

“Justice does not discriminate based on the perpetrator’s skin colour, lineage, or religion; indeed, injustice must be opposed, even when committed by those of the same race, religion, or political persuasion,” he added.
Meanwhile, Sabah Pakatan Harapan (PH) chairman Datuk Mustapha Sakmud described Abdul Hadi’s statement as extreme, out of bounds and completely unacceptable.

“Such remarks not only offend followers of other religions, but could also disrupt the harmony of Malaysia’s multiracial society, particularly in Sabah and Sarawak, which have long lived in an atmosphere of mutual respect regardless of religion, race and culture.
“In Sabah, there is no place for politics that discriminates against followers of other religions, as religious differences are not a barrier to family ties, friendship and community life,” he said.
He said a family in Sabah can have members who practise different faiths, yet they still live in harmony and mutual respect.

Mustapha stressed that Islam teaches its followers to be just to all people regardless of religion, adding that a leader’s justice or tyranny must be judged by their actions and integrity, not the faith they profess.
“As a political leader and religious figure, Abdul Hadi should act responsibly and refrain from making statements that could arouse prejudice and undermine social harmony,” he said.
Mustapha urged Sabahans and all Malaysians, particularly the people of Melaka, to remain vigilant and reject political parties that preach hatred against followers of other religions. — Bernama

fa67c5920455837f: Microsoft products including Outlook were out of action globally on November 13 2026. Alex Photo Stock/ShutterstockWhen I arrived at work to discover that Outlook had vanished from my computer, I wondered how I was supposed to get through my working day. No emails. No calendar. No meeting invitations. Then another thought crossed my mind: when did we become so dependent on a single technology company that losing access to one application could disrupt our entire working routine? And what is the financial and environmental cost of that dependence? We regularly discuss sustainability in terms of reducing plastic, cutting carbon emissions and consuming less energy. But the digital systems we rely on every day also have huge environmental consequences. As world leaders gather at the UN climate summit, Cop31, in Turkey, perhaps it is time to ask an uncomfortable question: can our digital economy really become sustainable when so much of it depends on a handful of technology companies? The cloud has a physical footprint The cloud may sound weightless, but it runs on data centres, electricity, cooling systems and hardware. The International Energy Agency estimates that data centres consumed 415 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2024, around 1.5% of global demand. It projects that consumption could reach 945 terawatt-hours by 2030, largely driven by AI and other digital services. Microsoft’s own 2026 sustainability report illustrates the tension. The company reported a 25% year-over-year rise in total emissions in 2025, primarily because of expanding data centres and a change in renewable-energy certificate accounting. Microsoft is also investing in cleaner energy and more efficient infrastructure. Both facts matter: technological progress can reduce emissions per task, while growth pushes overall demand higher. Asking the right questions Turkey’s Cop31 presidency released the voluntary Antalya artificial intelligence pledge in October. This pledge aims to encourage climate-responsible AI while acknowledging the energy and water demands of the technology. The World Resources Institute, a global research organisation, welcomed the pledge’s direction but warned that voluntary commitments need stronger accountability mechanisms. Meanwhile, the International Telecommunication Union has scheduled a Cop31 event for November 16 on financing cleaner digital infrastructure, measuring emissions, and promoting durable, repairable and reusable electronics. The message is important: sustainability cannot stop at greener electricity. It also concerns what technology organisations purchase, how long they keep it, and who pays for its environmental effects. When a software decision becomes a hardware bill Consider a computer that still works but cannot support a newer operating system. Windows 10’s regular support ended in October 2025, although Microsoft offers extended security updates for eligible consumer devices through October 2027. The transition does not make every older computer obsolete. Yet software support and compatibility can influence whether organisations replace otherwise usable equipment. Manufacturing devices consumes energy and raw materials. It also creates electronic waste (e-waste). According to the UN’s global e-waste monitor, the world generated 62 million metric tonnes of e-waste in 2022, of which just 22.3% was documented as formally collected and recycled. These figures cover all electronic waste, not waste attributable to Microsoft. They nevertheless show why extending equipment lifetimes deserves a place in climate policy. What are the environmental costs of using data and digital? Costs that are rarely counted A software subscription has a visible price. Less visible are the costs of training employees, migrating files, replacing equipment, maintaining duplicate systems and eventually switching suppliers. Economists call these switching costs. They can lock organisations into existing providers even when better-value alternatives emerge. This is not merely hypothetical. In March 2026, the UK’s Competition and Markets Authority announced plans to investigate Microsoft’s business software ecosystem. It also reported steps by major cloud service providers, including Microsoft Azure and Amazon Web Services, to reduce data-transfer fees and improve interoperability, making it easier for businesses to switch between providers. What might this have to do with sustainability? A buyer unable to change providers easily may also struggle to choose lower-emission computing services. That is a potential environmental consequence of lock-in, not a demonstrated claim that Microsoft users emit more carbon. There is a wider accounting problem too. The UN estimates that global electronic waste was associated with approximately US$78 billion (£59 billion) in externalised costs in 2022, including pollution and climate-related impacts. Such costs are largely absent from the price of a software license. A responsible procurement decision should therefore compare lifetime financial costs, equipment lifespans and credible emissions data rather than only the next annual bill. Freedom to choose Could workplaces use alternatives (such as Thunderbird and LibreOffice) or interoperable cloud services? Often, yes. But migration has costs and a rival provider is not necessarily greener. The better goal is freedom to choose: portable data, open document formats, repairable devices, transparent environmental reporting and software contracts that do not penalise switching. Digital systems that remain affordable, competitive and environmentally responsible, even when their preferred technology changes, will be the most resilient ones. Narmin Nahidi does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

95de0248ce79c8c9: PETALING JAYA: The market capitalisation of YTL Power International Bhd has plummeted by over RM8 billion in the past fortnight amid the turmoil at its US data centre partner Nvidia.

The multi-utility and infrastructure company saw over RM3 billion wiped off its market capitalisation yesterday when its shares fell over 8% or 39 sen to RM4.40, following reports of another extramarital affair of Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang, who quit his posts at the chipmaker yesterday.

Since US newspapers revealed his affair with an alleged Chinese spy at the end of October, YTL Power’s shares have dropped 18.2% from RM5.32 to RM4.35 today, erasing RM8.71 billion from its market valuation.
The stock closed five sen or 1.1% lower at RM4.35, giving it a market capitalisation of RM38.05 billion.

YTL Power operates Malaysia’s first Nvidia-powered AI data centre at the YTL Green Data Center Park in Kulai, Johor. The facility is equipped with some of the most advanced AI chips from Nvidia, the second most valuable company in the world behind Apple.
CGS International said the recent sell-off in YTL Power “appears excessive” as its colocation data centre business continues to support the group's valuation.
The research house cited improving near-term earnings and longer-term growth prospects that it believes are not fully reflected in the share price.
“We believe it is important to distinguish YTL Power’s contracted colocation business from its broader AI data centre ambitions,” it said in a recent note.
CGS maintained its “add” rating with an optimistic target price of RM6.50, staying bullish despite pressure from Nvidia-related concerns and tighter scrutiny of AI chip supply chains.
The alleged spy, a senior executive of Singapore-based Megaspeed International, has been accused of helping entities circumvent US restrictions on imports of high-performance chips to China.
News reports say she facilitated the shipment of at least US$7.5 billion (RM30.6 billion) worth of Nvidia chips to Chinese firms.
Megaspeed, which has a Malaysian unit Speedmatrix Sdn Bhd, is now under investigation by the US and Singapore.
Malaysia is ready to facilitate any formal request to investigate Speedmatrix, said investment, trade and industry minister Johari Ghani yesterday.
However, he added the government has yet to receive any such request.
It was reported that Speedmatrix might have breached the country’s export restrictions.
YTL Power’s business covers power, water, telecommunications, and digital infrastructure sectors. It also operates in Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand, China, the UK, the Netherlands and Jordan.

78ce30f51762c48a: SHAH ALAM, Nov 13 — The Selangor government has allocated RM36.45 million for 47 immediate flood mitigation projects under the Department of Irrigation and Drainage (JPS) for 2027.

Menteri Besar Datuk Seri Amirudin Shari, when tabling the state’s Budget 2027, said that of the total, RM9.15 million would be for the Sungai Klang basin and RM7.35 million for the development of the Sungai Langat basin.
He said the allocation would also cover the Sungai Buloh, Sungai Selangor, Sungai Bernam and Sungai Kapar Besar river basins, as well as preparatory works such as design, surveying and land matters.

He added that, of the 47 projects, 30 are continuation projects, of which 13 have been completed and are undergoing final account preparation, nine are being implemented, two are at the pre-tender stage while six are at the design stage.

“As for the 17 new projects, one is at the design stage, 11 are in the process of appointing consultants and five are still at the planning stage,” he said at the Selangor State Legislative Assembly sitting today.

Amirudin also said that RM19.38 million had been allocated for 25 irrigation system projects, RM17.90 million for 16 river basin development and management projects, and RM6.63 million for nine environmentally friendly irrigation projects.

For flood mitigation projects under the Selangor Maritime Gateway Economic Development Zone (SMG ZPE), RM25 million has been proposed to continue works to increase river capacity and improve water flow, with the projects having achieved 71.43 per cent physical progress.
While physical works are underway, Amirudin said the disaster warning system between the state and district operation centres and agencies on the ground would also be improved.

“Through the Community-Based Disaster Risk Management Programme and training in schools, we want residents to know where they need to go, who to contact and how to assist those who need support to evacuate,” he added.
Amirudin also wants the Public Works Department (JKR), local authorities (PBTs) and the JPS to prioritise projects that resolves flooding problems, including culverts and drainage systems.

“Technical reviews that can be conducted concurrently should be initiated simultaneously. If a decision involves multiple agencies, the matter must be brought to the relevant authorities who can resolve it at an earlier stage.

“The Netherlands’ experience offers us a guide on what needs to be accelerated and one of the initiatives is the integration of embankments and water control structures with planning that allows rivers to overflow more safely,” he added.

Meanwhile, he said the state government would provide a public dashboard displaying project locations, implementing agencies and updates on implementation phases, from the appointment of design consultants and contractors to the progress of on-site works.

“Before the monsoon season begins, the government will update the status of flood-prone locations, detailing the related projects, appointments that have been made and works expected to be completed in time.
“With this information, residents can know the level of protection in their areas ahead of the rainy season and refer directly to the agencies responsible,” he said. — Bernama
58d49ba4b49b1f23: Look, off in the ether – is it a bird, is it a plane? No, it's a stupid idea, on final approach...
And look, the Boss has his office door open!
C L E A R A N C E T O L A N D !

The Boss has wandered into Mission Control with something obviously on his mind. Over time, the PFY and I have learned to equate these thoughtful moments with the BAG FULL lamp of a commercial vacuum cleaner at a waxing salon. Do not open.

His presence in Mission Control is never a good sign, but his "thoughtful" presence, even more so. He'll have seen something, read something, spoken to someone, or possibly overheard something in a toilet stall that will have sounded – to him – like a great idea. Or it might have been a cheddar-frenzy-induced fever dream that he wants to run by us.
And the Boss's crazy ideas are, unfortunately, like bran flakes to his mental digestion, the output of which being delivered to the PFY and myself as a veritable slurry of poorly considered ideas.
"AI," he says, pausing for effect, once he's rolled to a stop.

He then waits patiently for one of us to ask "What about AI?" However, that will never happen. In terms of stupidity, it's up there with saying Candyman into a mirror five times, power washing a gremlin, or visiting a basement when Jason's in town.
"For the security system," the Boss teases.
I continue my intense focus on my monitors, hoping the lunacy will depart. The PFY does the same.
The PFY and I know that the only way out of this is to stall till the end of the day, at which time the Boss's overnight reset will trigger, leaving him only a vague memory of having had a good idea.
>clickety< >tap<
"Uh-oh," I say, reaching into my drawer for my crashtop. "It looks like one of the distribution switches on 4 has crashed."
>tappity<
"And not just 4 – it looks like the boardroom has gone down too."
"It could be a virus," I say, using words I know the Boss will respond to.
"A virus?!" the Boss gasps.
"I don't know. It's too soon to tell," I say, departing.

So now I'm hiding in a cramped comms room on the fourth floor while I plug the crashtop into the CCTV VLAN so I can check on the Boss's location. Luckily, we upgraded the system to an AI-integrated platform, so I only need to type IDIOT into the search field to find him.
Sure enough, he's back in his office, typing away furiously, which can only mean there's a memo on its way. And if there's a memo, there's a path to reminding him of his dumb idea tomorrow...
>tappity< >tap< >tap< >clickety<
On the screen, the Boss looks around anxiously as his laptop fires up DBAN in full confirm mode. He then reaches for a sheet of paper and starts scribbling furiously.
>tappity< >tap<
The office lights switch off as the BMS system clock suddenly finds out that it's midnight.
On the screen, the Boss's phone torch comes on and he resumes scribbling.
>bip< >bip< >bip< >biiiiiiip<
>ring<
"Hello?" the Boss asks, with a hint of feedback.
"It's the virus!" I gasp. "It's coming from inside the building!!!"
Meantime, I've messaged the PFY and advised him to pick up the shredder from the boardroom cupboard.
"What do I do?" the Boss gasps.
"It's the wireless broadband connection on the roof!" I say. "We need to disconnect it!"
"I thought you said it was coming from inside the building?" the Boss asks.
DAMMIT!
>tappity< >click< >tap< >tap<
Further discussion is impossible now that his phone is erasing itself, having been marked as a stolen device...
The PFY was unable to find the shredder, as it looks to have been dumped now that board papers are no longer printed. On the plus side, he has a plan.
...two hours later...
"So, we're clear to enter the building?" I ask the fire warden.
"Yes, you're clear, though it looks like the fire started on your floor."
"It doesn't surprise me," I say. "We're creative people. Our ideas spark innovation."
"It looks like there was some as-yet-unknown accelerant used."
"Really? Was it... enthusiasm?" I ask.
"No, more like lighter fluid."
"Oh," I say, thinking of the smokers the PFY occasionally chats to outside at the skip. "Well, we may never know."
"Don't you have some sort of AI surveillance system?" he asks.
"Sadly, that was the first thing to go," I lie.
...Later, in Mission Control...
"So, in review," the PFY says. "We shut down a couple of switches, put the building in night mode, trashed a laptop and a mobile phone, then set fire to the building."
"Yes."
"Simply to stop a dumb idea?"
"Yes."
"And the funny thing is, I took a look at his scribblings – and it wasn't all that bad."
"Really?" I ask, reaching for the isopropyl and a lighter, just in case it's contagious.

a53f3a7a4226f241: Britain's privacy watchdog has put healthcare bosses on notice after receiving more than 300 reports of staff snooping through medical records this year, demanding that executives personally confirm they're doing enough to keep prying eyes out of patient files.

The Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) said on Thursday that it had written to more than 200 senior health leaders across the UK, warning that employees accessing records without good reason put patient privacy and public trust at risk.

The ICO received and assessed more than 300 reports of medical record snooping between January and mid-October 2026. Staff were caught looking up people they knew, poking around patient files out of sheer curiosity, and sharing private information with people who had no business seeing it.
The figure covers reports submitted by healthcare organizations rather than confirmed breaches, and excludes cases still awaiting assessment.
ICO chief executive Paul Arnold wants health bosses to personally assure him that their organizations have safeguards in place to stop staff having a nose through records they aren't supposed to see.

"Accessing someone's health records without a legitimate reason isn't harmless curiosity. It can cause enormous distress to patients and jeopardize the vital trust people place in our health service," Arnold said.

In a three-page letter to chief executives, Arnold makes clear that simply trusting staff to behave themselves won't cut it. He wants to know who can access patient records, whether anyone is checking what they're looking at, and what happens when somebody gets caught snooping.

Health bosses are also expected to investigate suspected breaches without dragging their feet, work out whether patients need to be told, and take action against staff caught accessing records they shouldn't.

Executives have until November 27 to respond. Those who haven't reviewed their safeguards in the past six months, or aren't happy with what they find, have been given another three months to put their house in order.

The problem isn't necessarily that healthcare workers are hacking into systems, as many already have legitimate access to patient records as part of their jobs. The trouble starts when they use that access to look up someone they're not treating, whether it's a neighbor, an ex-partner, or somebody whose name has appeared in the news.

This isn't the first time health authorities have tried to stamp out the problem. In July, NHS England warned employees that accessing records without a legitimate reason could cost them their jobs or even land them in prison.

That crackdown followed incidents involving staff accessing the medical records of victims of high-profile crimes, including the Nottingham attacks. NHS England also published guidance encouraging organizations to use access controls and audit systems to catch employees poking around where they shouldn't.

Some newer electronic patient record systems can even flag suspicious access in real time, although the NHS acknowledged that monitoring capabilities vary depending on the technology organizations have installed.

The scale of the problem has been troubling regulators for years. In July, the UK government told Parliament that 1,445 cases of inappropriate access had been reported to the ICO between 2019 and 2025.

And the consequences can go beyond getting the sack. The ICO has prosecuted 16 healthcare workers for snooping through patient records over the past decade, with unauthorized access to personal information potentially amounting to a criminal offense under the Data Protection Act 2018.
Arnold warned that the regulator could also take enforcement action against healthcare organizations whose protections aren't up to scratch.
"I've written to chief executives across the UK asking them to personally assure me that their safeguards work in practice. Where they don't, we expect organizations to put that right," he said.
With hundreds of reports already landing on the watchdog's desk this year, healthcare bosses now have a fortnight to explain how they're keeping staff out of records they have no business reading. ®

What happened before this

On December 7, 2017, 18-year-old Smit was found nude and dead on the sixth floor of CapSquare Residence, a condominium off Jalan Dang Wangi in Kuala Lumpur, after having fallen from a unit on the 20th floor.
The Coroner’s Court on March 18, 2019 in an inquest found that Smit’s death was caused by a “misadventure”.
But the High Court on November 22, 2019 replaced the inquest findings by saying that Smit’s death was caused by “a person or persons unknown”, and ordered the police to start investigations again.

In November 2020, Smit’s mother Christina Carolina Gerarda Johanna Verstappen filed a civil suit against the inspector-general of police, Dang Wangi investigating officer ASP Faizal Abdullah, the home minister, and the Malaysian government over alleged breach of duties and negligence in investigating the cause of her daughter’s 2017 death.

On July 29, 2025, the High Court ordered all those sued to pay RM1.1 million compensation, and declared the police as having failed to carry out their duties to restart investigations as ordered in 2019.

Also on July 29, 2025, the High Court issued a court order known as a “mandamus order”, which included ordering the police to restart investigations on Smit’s death and to brief the Attorney General’s Chambers every three months with updates on the investigation.
On October 14, 2026, the Court of Appeal set aside the High Court’s decision, including the RM1.1 million award.

Among other things, the Court of Appeal reportedly ruled that the police’s public duty to investigate crime does not give rise to a private duty of care that would result in compensation to individual victims or their relatives for perceived investigation failures.

The Court of Appeal had also ruled that the decisions from the inquest and the 2019 criminal revision at the High Court could not by themselves establish civil liability in a separate case, Sankara said today.

In his statement today, Sankara also said the Court of Appeal’s October 14 decision does not mean that public authorities would have blanket immunity, but said it is a “substantial obstacle” for families who are pursuing such court claims over alleged negligence in investigations of deaths.

“We respectfully recognise the courts’ responsibility to apply established legal principles. Nevertheless, concerns about exposing public authorities to excessive litigation must be weighed against the need for meaningful accountability.

“A public duty must carry practical substance for the people it exists to protect. Where the law restricts civil redress, the case for effective independent oversight and legislative consideration becomes all the more pressing and compelling,” he said in the same statement.

4991fecb9b069f6e: NOVEMBER 13 — When Pakatan Harapan (PH) announced its young candidate for the Kuala Linggi state constituency in Melaka, public scepticism was almost instantaneous. Muhammad Mukhlisul Mubin Julasapiyah, a young law graduate, soon found himself at the receiving end of online ridicule, with social media users casually dismissing him as budak mentah, budak tak matang, budak tak ada pengalaman, budak tak tahu apa-apa. The familiar vocabulary of condescension, delivered with remarkable confidence by those who seem convinced that age is the ultimate measure of competence.

Once again, why are we so sceptical of the young? What exactly is wrong with someone in his twenties aspiring to represent his community? Since when has political maturity become the exclusive privilege of those who have spent decades occupying positions of authority?

Amanah president Datuk Seri Mohamad Sabu (left) spends time with Pakatan Harapan candidate for the Kuala Linggi state seat, Muhammad Mukhlisul Mubin Julasapiyah, during a Pakatan Harapan talk at Jalan Telok Gong, Pengkalan Balak, Alor Gajah on October 2, 2026. — Bernama pic

There is something deeply peculiar about Malaysia's relationship with its younger generation. We call them the nation's future, applaud their enthusiasm and eagerly enlist them to campaign for seasoned politicians. Yet the moment they aspire to power themselves, the applause gives way to suspicion. Apparently, young people are sufficiently mature to deliver votes, though somehow too immature to deserve them.

What troubles me most is the arrogance behind this attitude. Seniority has become a convenient substitute for intellectual authority. Experience is invoked as though it were a hereditary title, bestowed by time and immune from scrutiny. How, then, can we demand experience from young people while guarding every doorway through which experience is acquired?

History makes this prejudice difficult to defend. Nelson Mandela helped establish the ANC Youth League at 26. Sanna Marin became Finland's prime minister at 34; Jacinda Ardern led New Zealand at 37. At home, Najib Razak entered Parliament at 23, Nurul Izzah Anwar won Lembah Pantai at 27, and Hannah Yeoh entered the Selangor assembly at 29. Their legacies vary. Their youth never prevented them from entering the arena.

Syed Saddiq Syed Abdul Rahman offers a more immediate example. He became a federal minister at 25 and helped push Undi18 into law, enlarging the democratic space for an entire generation. In Muar, he turned to unconventional fundraising when resources were needed. His ThunderBOLD initiative raised RM196,668 for tablets for disadvantaged students. Critics called such efforts publicity stunts. Perhaps. Yet how many representatives who mock these methods can point to comparable ingenuity in serving their constituents? Political leadership should be measured by what it delivers, rather than its obedience to old habits.

Young leaders can bring urgency, technological fluency, intellectual curiosity and a willingness to question arrangements others have mistaken for permanent truths. Youth itself guarantees none of these qualities. Neither does growing old confer wisdom. And that is precisely why our reverence for political longevity is so troubling.

Are we seriously unmoved by the same political faces being recycled since the 1980s? The same feuds, the same manoeuvres, the same exhausted ideas dressed in the language of renewal. When experience hardens into complacency, it ceases to be an advantage. A country cannot think its way into the future with leaders who insist on living indefinitely in the past.

Take Marang. According to MyPoliticians' Hansard-based records, Abdul Hadi Awang, now 79, attended approximately 24 per cent of 249 Dewan Rakyat sittings recorded through March 2026. Attendance alone cannot capture every contribution or explain every absence, although such a record plainly invites accountability. Why are we so eager to interrogate a young candidate's hypothetical shortcomings while remaining curiously indulgent towards the measurable performance of established figures?

Malaysia should begin debating term limits and serious standards of legislative accountability. Even proposals for age-related restrictions deserve careful discussion, though any threshold must respect democratic rights and avoid replacing one prejudice with another. The essential principle is simple: public office should never become a lifetime reservation. Leadership requires fresh ideas, endurance and the humility to know when to make way.

I know the cost of this mentality personally. I became a lecturer at 26 and encountered a senior colleague who repeatedly doubted my ability without a credible basis. What made it harder to swallow was the air of superiority from someone whose own competence, to my mind, scarcely justified it. Eventually, I caught myself holding back, reluctant to excel because excellence seemed to provoke resentment. Imagine how many capable young Malaysians have learnt to make themselves smaller merely to keep someone senior comfortable. This is how institutions suffocate talent, quietly and then systematically.

Perhaps Sukarno understood something we have conveniently forgotten when he declared: “Beri aku 1.000 orang tua, niscaya akan kucabut Semeru dari akarnya. Beri aku 10 pemuda, niscaya akan kuguncangkan dunia.” His words captured the extraordinary transformative power of youth. Yet here we are, still questioning their capabilities, dismissing their potential and expecting them to remain in the shadows of their seniors. How can a nation aspire to progress when it remains so reluctant to trust the very generation that will inherit its future?

The least we can do is give them the opportunity to prove themselves. Let the young contest, lead and prove themselves. Judge their ideas, character and work. Malaysia has spent far too long asking whether the young are mature enough to lead. Perhaps it is time to ask whether the old guard is mature enough to make way.

* Shah Mohd Akmal Abdul Halim is a lecturer in the Department of Social Sciences and Humanities, College of Continuing Education (CCEd), Universiti Tenaga Nasional (UNITEN), and a PhD candidate at the Institute of Ethnic Studies (KITA), Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia (UKM).

01fd00249e6ebcc4: PARIS: Global oil supplies are expected to exceed demand in the fourth quarter, after increased Gulf exports led to a market surplus in October for the first time since the Iran war, the International Energy Agency said Friday.

"The oil market is showing tentative signs of rebalancing, with global oil supplies surpassing demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war in Iran," the IEA said.

Prices have fallen sharply in recent weeks as Tehran has begun allowing more vessels that obtain its authorisation to traverse the Strait of Hormuz, which it effectively closed in the initial months of the war launched by the US and Israel in late February.
That helped overall oil supply to rise by three million barrels per day in September and a further 2.3 million barrels in October, the IEA said.
But global demand is set to fall by 2.7 mb/d overall this year as oil prices remain well above pre-war levels and "accelerate electrification and fuel efficiencies across the global car fleet".
Diesel prices in particular stood at US$180 per barrel in October, around 77% higher than before the war, as Iran struck refineries in neighbouring Gulf countries accused of aiding US attacks.
Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries and other energy installations are also disrupting diesel supplies to the global market.
"The severe tightness in product supply, especially for diesel, remains the overriding concern of the broader market and consumers," the IEA said.

4b96fcf598674f14: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 13 — The future of Malaysia is taking shape today: not inside corporate boardrooms, but across the classrooms, technical workshops and community spaces where young minds are learning to solve real-world challenges.

Across the nation, a rising generation of students and vocational trainees is gaining more than theoretical knowledge; they are acquiring the practical skills and confidence needed to take decisive action. Increasingly, they are being met with the platforms and mentorship to do so.

Two flagship initiatives by UMW Toyota Motor illustrate how this philosophy works in practice: the Toyota Eco Youth (TEY) programme, now in its 25th edition, and the Toyota Technical Education Program (T-TEP), which has nurtured local automotive talent since 1991.
Together, they champion a straightforward principle: when young Malaysians are entrusted with the right tools and guidance, they consistently rise to the occasion.
Turning environmental awareness into action

The TEY programme, run in collaboration with the Ministry of Education, challenges secondary school students aged 13 to 16 to observe their surroundings and confront a crucial question: what environmental problem in our community needs an urgent solution?
This year, 327 project proposals were submitted by schools nationwide, from which 30 teams were shortlisted to take their ideas into their communities.
What distinguishes TEY is its emphasis on execution.

Shortlisted teams work through Toyota's eight-step Problem Solving Methodology (PSM): identifying and selecting a problem, understanding the current situation, setting a target, analysing the root cause, drafting countermeasures, implementing them, checking the results and finally standardising the solution so it lasts.
The results are already visible.

At Sekolah Menengah Sains Seri Puteri (SESERI) in Kuala Lumpur, four Form Four students behind the ScrubCycle project are tackling a habit many households take for granted: pouring used cooking oil down the sink.
The team developed an eco bar soap-making kit that lets residents turn their used oil into soap, with workshops that stress the safe handling of materials.
At the Malay College Kuala Kangsar (MCKK), a team of four Form Four students called MC Kitar4Impact used TEY 2026 to take an earlier competition idea into the real world.
Their platform, GoKitar, lets retailers sell groceries that are still safe to use at lower prices, or channel them to charity.
It is now being piloted with five local retailers and a community partner, with the team aiming to save at least 300 products from going to waste.

Guided by teacher-advisors and technical mentors, participants learn to manage projects from ideation through to measurable results, and to see themselves as capable changemakers in their own communities.
Skills that open career pathways
While TEY fosters environmental stewardship, T-TEP focuses on developing Malaysia's future automotive workforce.

Established in line with the government's push to close the gap between education and industry expectations, the programme integrates Toyota's syllabus into partner institutions, supplies training equipment and opens up internship and employment opportunities for students.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Students gain hands-on automotive experience as part of technical training designed to prepare them for real-world industry requirements. — Picture courtesy of UMW Toyota Motor
What began with five institutions has now grown to 25 technical and vocational education and training (TVET) institutes.

They include Kolej Vokasional campuses under the Ministry of Education, TVETMARA colleges under Majlis Amanah Rakyat (MARA), Universiti Kuala Lumpur's Malaysia France Institute, IKTBN Dusun Tua, and private colleges such as KISMEC in Sungai Petani and Kolej TAFE in Seremban.
The network spans the peninsula as well as Sabah and Sarawak.
UMW Toyota Motor is backing the expansion with an RM8.4 million investment covering training equipment for the institutes and internship allowances for students.
For students, the centrepiece of T-TEP is a six-month on-the-job training placement at Toyota and Lexus service centres nationwide, with some 300 trainees expected to go through it each year.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
T-TEP trainees visit a Toyota service centre, where students gain exposure to real-world automotive operations and on-the-job training. — Picture courtesy of UMW Toyota Motor

Trainees can name their preferred dealers and receive a monthly allowance. At each dealer, they rotate through the roles of technician, service advisor and parts assistant, with a mentor assigned at each stage.
On the general service track, trainees progress from inspection and routine servicing to repairs and basic diagnosis before moving to frontline service and parts.
Body and paint trainees move from panel beating and surface preparation to painting, final quality checks and frontline service.
The programme already has results to show, having reached some 2,500 students and trained 500 interns, 250 of whom were subsequently hired.
T-TEP is also part of a global Toyota programme supporting technical institutions worldwide, with distributors and dealers helping partner institutes keep pace with advances in automotive technology.
At their core, both initiatives are anchored in the conviction that investing in youth is fundamental to nation-building.

Environmental innovation and technical craftsmanship may appear to be separate disciplines, yet both empower young Malaysians to identify pressing problems and solve them with purpose, skill and confidence.
T-TEP is helping to lift young Malaysian talents to global standards.
While corporate initiatives provide the essential resources, training frameworks and mentorship platforms, the real credit belongs to the students, trainees and educators themselves.
They are the ones taking initiative, validating solutions and building the foundation for a more skilled, sustainable Malaysia.

23aeec9c1675b4a2: NOVEMBER 13 — Every generation believes the one after it has it easier, and the one before it simply does not understand. Older Malaysians complain that the young are fragile, impatient and glued to their phones. Younger Malaysians roll their eyes at “boomers” who lecture them about hard work while owning homes they bought decades ago. Both caricatures contain a grain of truth. Both are also, in the end, unfair.

I am 62, a senior citizen and a person with disability. I have lived long enough to see the world change several times over, and I have learned that most of what we call a generation gap is really a gap in circumstances.

I grew up in Kuala Rompin, Pahang, where I learned Jawi from my late father and read Utusan Melayu in Jawi script from the age of four. Libraries were my second home. After an intensive English course at ITM, I was sent to New Zealand, where I studied at the University of Waikato and followed the 1984 general election closely as a student.

My first job was in information technology at TV3. In 1993, I began writing a newspaper column titled “Sebuah Komputer Setiap Rumah”, arguing that every Malaysian home should have a computer, at a time when few Malaysian homes had one. I later spent nearly two decades working in Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, including at Dubai Internet City in its early years.

I say all this not to boast, but to make a point: my generation was not more virtuous than today’s young people. We were luckier in certain ways. We came of age when a degree, a stable job, marriage and a home could reasonably be expected to follow one another in sequence. For many young Malaysians today, that sequence has broken down.

The generation gap will never disappear, and perhaps it should not. Each generation must answer the questions of its own time. But a gap is not the same as a divide. A gap can be bridged by curiosity, listening and shared purpose. A divide is what we create when we stop trying. — Picture by Sayuti Zainudin

The numbers tell the story. Malaysia recorded 396,175 live births in 2025, and the total fertility rate fell to just 1.5 children per woman. The Khazanah Research Institute has described the housing market as seriously unaffordable, with home prices growing at more than double the rate of median household income. When young people delay marriage, postpone children or rent indefinitely, it is too easy for my generation to call it selfishness. More often, it is arithmetic.

At the same time, the country is growing old. About 4.2 million Malaysians are now aged 60 and above, and Malaysia is expected to become an aged nation by 2036. My generation will need more care, more health services and more patience from the young, just as the young are struggling to build their own lives. If we approach this with mutual suspicion, both sides will lose.
So what should older Malaysians learn from the young?

First, humility about technology. The young did not invent the smartphone to annoy us. Today, I depend on a ride-hailing app to move around, and I make short daily videos on TikTok about life after 60. Neither would have been possible without tools built and popularised largely by younger people. Older Malaysians who refuse to learn a new app on principle should remember that, not so long ago, it was our generation telling our own elders to embrace the computer.

Second, respect for their values, even when they differ from ours. Many young Malaysians care deeply about mental health, work-life balance, the environment and fairness. These are not signs of weakness. They are often signs of a generation that watched its parents sacrifice health and family for careers that did not always reward them.
And what can the young learn from us?

Perspective, mostly. Many of us lived through recessions, political upheavals and the long, slow building of a nation. We know that difficult periods pass, that institutions can be reformed, and that patience is not the same as passivity. We also carry memories that no search engine can provide: of kampung life, of languages and scripts that are fading, of how communities looked after one another before welfare agencies existed. When an older person dies, a library of lived experience closes with them.

Bridging the gap requires more than goodwill. It requires deliberate design. Senior activity centres could invite university students to teach digital skills, while seniors mentor young people in crafts, languages, local history and career experience. Housing policy could encourage multigenerational living rather than penalise it. Workplaces could pair older and younger employees in reverse mentoring, so that each learns from the other. Schools could record oral histories from grandparents before those stories are lost.

Families matter most of all. My three sons studied abroad and now work as managers. Their world is very different from the one I grew up in, and I have had to learn to listen more and advise less. I have also had to face honest questions about my own old age, including visiting elderly care centres and realising how costly such care can be. These are conversations that every family will need to have, and they go better when both generations come to the table with respect rather than resentment.

The generation gap will never disappear, and perhaps it should not. Each generation must answer the questions of its own time. But a gap is not the same as a divide. A gap can be bridged by curiosity, listening and shared purpose. A divide is what we create when we stop trying.
In a Malaysia that is ageing fast and having fewer children, can we really afford for the old and the young to stop listening to each other?
