e67209abafcd865a: Coastal wetlands, such as mangroves and saltmarshes, are rapidly disappearing yet they are incredibly important for young turtles. In a new study, my colleagues and I used satellite tags to track young green turtles in a protected wetland in Sharjah, UAE. Our results reveal just how important these remaining natural spaces are to young turtles. But we also found that nature can find a way to thrive in unexpected, human-made environments too. So protecting these habitats and the connections between wetlands, artificial environments and the open sea is essential to ensuring wildlife can persist in an increasingly human-shaped world. Coastal wetlands protect our shorelines from storms, store carbon and provide important nursery habitats for marine life. Yet scientists still know surprisingly little about how marine wildlife, including turtles, sharks and rays, use these environments. Knowing where these animals feed, shelter and move helps identify which areas need protection and whether existing protected areas are working. Our study, a collaborative effort between the Environment and Protected Areas Authority (EPAA), a UAE government agency, the University of Exeter and the Sharjah Marine Science Research Centre, focused on Al Qurm Wa Lehhfaiiah, a marine protected area encompassing the last major coastal wetland ecosystem on the UAE’s east coast, which is called Khor Kalba. Its complex wetlands support migratory wading birds, numerous fish species and the Arabian collared kingfisher, a subspecies found only in this region. Young green turtles also swim through its winding mangrove channels. Although the wetland is now protected and recognised as a Ramsar site, a type of conservation designation for any internationally important wetlands, it has not escaped human development. The city of Kalba surrounds much of the site, and a large human-made basin (like a lagoon) was built alongside the natural mangroves in the early 2000s as a proposed recreational and commercial waterfront. The basin was never used for its intended recreational purposes and has since been incorporated into the protected area. To understand how young turtles use this unusual landscape alongside the natural mangrove channels, EPAA staff carefully captured nine juvenile green turtles in 2019 and attached satellite tags to their shells using a specialist, harmless resin. After the turtles were released, the tags allowed us to follow their movements. After seven months and over 2,800 satellite locations the results were clear. We found Kalba’s wetlands were a critical habitat for all nine turtles. They generally stayed within just 2 miles of the wetland entrance and spent more than 80% of their tracked time inside the marine protected area’s boundary. Basin benefits One of the more surprising findings was the popularity of the human-made basin (similar to a saltwater lagoon extending from the mangroves). The turtles were around five times more likely to be found there than elsewhere in the wetland, and 77% of their core-use areas were concentrated within it. We cannot say for certain why the turtles favoured the basin. One possibility is that algae growing on its floor provides food, while its enclosed layout may offer shelter from larger predators. Whatever the explanation, the findings suggest that wildlife can make use of human-modified environments. However, this is no substitute for protecting natural habitats. Where coastal environments are modified or restored, designs that retain natural habitats, maintain connections between them and preserve the ecological processes they depend on may offer the greatest benefits for wildlife. One turtle eventually embarked on a very different journey. After remaining in the wetland for 93 days, it travelled over 500 miles to Masirah Island in neighbouring Oman. This remarkable journey highlights how a small coastal wetland can be important to young turtles before they move into wider waters. But the study also revealed a gap in protection. The main natural channel connecting the ocean to the mangroves and basin currently lies outside the marine protected area. Although the turtles used this channel less frequently overall, they gathered there at low tide, possibly waiting for rising water to allow them to move back into the wetland. Extending protection to include this connecting channel could therefore strengthen the conservation value of the entire system. Our findings underline the importance of protecting natural coastal wetlands. The human-made basin may offer unexpected benefits, but the natural mangrove channels and their connection to the sea remain essential parts of the wider ecosystem. As coastal development continues around the world, understanding how wildlife uses both natural and modified environments can help us make better conservation decisions. Protecting the remaining wetlands at Kalba, including the connections between them and the ocean, is an important step towards securing a future for the young turtles that depend on them. Owen Exeter receives funding from the Environment and Protected Areas Authority (EPAA), the University of Exeter and the Sharjah Marine Science Research Centre.
58fc2a20b65c25a8: UK police forces must do more to prevent the wrongful arrests of people subjected to retrospective facial recognition (RFR) searches, according to a Criminal Justice Inspectorate that holds deep concerns about the way in which the technology is used.

According to a report from His Majesty's Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Services (HMICFRS), there is a large gap in understanding among police forces and the National Crime Agency about how RFR should be used in responsible policing.
The inspectorate blamed "fragmented and underdeveloped" frameworks for governance and legislation.

It pointed to a lack of bespoke legislation to provide a uniform approach to police facial recognition use – and said existing laws have not kept pace with the technology. HMICFRS also said the rules governing each force's use of RFR are mismatched, and called for a statutory code to be included in the forthcoming Police Reform Bill to set nationwide standards.

Illustrating the breadth of misunderstanding across forces, the report noted that despite the message being routinely communicated by National Police Chiefs' Council (NPCC) reps, individual investigators "often" thought RFR results constituted evidence rather than intelligence.
In many cases, they are unaware that RFR results require further enquiries before enforcement action can be taken.

"We found that some investigators didn't always carry out enough corroborative enquiries before acting on potential matches," the report stated. "In a small number of cases, officers relied too heavily on RFR results, which led to inappropriate investigative action.
"Although some forces had strengthened their processes after such incidents, practice remained inconsistent."
Later in the report, the inspectorate described the findings as "deeply concerning."

Some of the excuses police staff offered included acute demands on response teams leading to reduced opportunities to carry out further enquiries before acting on RFR matches. In one force, managers were known to encourage officers to "progress investigations quickly" after getting a match on the RFR system.
However, the inspectorate clarified that just because an arrest is made, it does not necessarily mean it is wrongful, as investigators may need to rule out subjects from their inquiries.
The onus for taking action should also be placed on the police forces themselves, given that some lack formal procedures regarding how RFR enquiries should be carried out, the report noted.
The best forces had centralized facial recognition teams, which generally provided better governance and consistent processes.
Officials fear long-term misuse of RFR, and other forms of facial recognition, will erode public trust in the technology, which it insists remains generally high.

Surveys carried out in 2025 by the likes of the Ada Lovelace Institute and Alan Turing Institute, as well as the King's College London Policy Institute, showed a generally favorable view of facial recognition use in UK policing, with support ranging from 91 percent and 53 percent respectively.
Home Office figures released on Thursday to complement the report show similar positivity toward the technology among police officers, with only 4 percent reporting a negative experience.
The Register's comments section often paints a vastly different picture of public perception of facial recognition.

Kathryn Stone, his majesty's inspector at HMICFRS, said facial recognition has transformed policing, allowing officers to compare images in seconds, allowing them to solve crimes more quickly, but echoed the report's main concerns.

"Police forces must be able to show that appropriate safeguards are in place, risks relating to bias and data retention are effectively managed, and decisions are still subject to human judgment," she said.
"A clearer statutory framework, stronger national standards and improved governance and oversight arrangements are essential to maintaining public confidence."

As well as legislative and governance-related concerns, HMICFRS also noted in its report that officers' training around the use of RFR remains inconsistent, and if improvements were made, this would lead to more effective and lawful use of RFR across the UK.

Another major issue was police forces' failure to meet their image retention obligations. Forces were found too often to retain custody images taken of suspects on the Police National Database, against which many RFR queries are made.
Police guidance sets out the scenarios in which custody images can and cannot be retained, and the inspectorate found that forces have failed to delete images that should have been wiped.

The Police Reform Bill includes a provision to group custody images with the likes of DNA and fingerprints, bringing about more robust measures to ensure they are retained or deleted in line with legal requirements.

A Home Office review previously found in 2017 that introducing such a statutory framework was untenable. It concluded that police could not automate the deletion of these images, and doing so manually would be too time-consuming.
Jasleen Chaggar, senior legal and policy officer at Big Brother Watch, said UK police cannot be allowed to continue to use RFR when it risks wrongfully arresting individuals.
"The revelations that officers are treating facial recognition as bona fide evidence rather than a probability score is alarming," she said.

"This approach significantly increases the risk that more innocent people will have officers knock on their door to arrest them for crimes committed in towns they've never visited, as we've seen before.

"Worse still, police aren't even logging their use of retrospective facial recognition, meaning people could wrongfully become suspects in criminal investigations without any record of why they've been accused."
Chaggar called on the government to "urgently step in" and help the UK's police forces to sort out the new frameworks needed for effective RFR use. ®
53bc70ad6b322e23: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 13 — The government has agreed today to maintain the existing minimum entry requirements for Unified Examination Certificate (UEC) holders seeking admission into medical programmes at private higher education institutions.
Communications Minister Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil said the decision was agreed to during a Cabinet meeting chaired by Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim today.
He said the decision is consistent with the government’s previous requirements and retains the same criteria that existed prior to any amendments.

Fahmi, who is also the unity government spokesman, said UEC holders who meet the minimum requirement of a ‘B4’ grade in five specified subjects remain eligible to apply for admission into medical degree programmes at private higher education institutions.
“The Cabinet agreed to maintain the minimum entry requirements for UEC holders intending to pursue medical programmes,” he said during a post-Cabinet media conference that was broadcast live today.
A B4 is the minimum UEC grade required in each of five compulsory subjects: Biology, Chemistry, Physics, and Mathematics (or Advanced Mathematics I and II, or Advanced Mathematics).

Fahmi added that the Health Ministry and the Malaysian Medical Council (MMC) will coordinate any administrative issues with the Higher Education Ministry to ensure the smooth implementation based on the decision.
He explained that the effort is intended to address any emerging issues.
“It is also to ensure that the standards and quality of medical education in the country, including at private higher education institutions, are upheld,” he said.
The UEC qualification remains unrecognised by the government as an entry qualification for admission to any public universities.

However, UEC holders remain eligible for direct admission into medical degree programmes (such as MBBS or MD) at private higher education institutions in Malaysia, provided they also meet SPM/UEC credit requirements for Bahasa Malaysia and English as mandated by MMC.

b57df9ce996b7895: Scientists have been working on ways to decode brain activity for decades. Teams have developed brain implants that can be used to control robotic limbs and computers, and even to “speak.”

The people who volunteer for trials of those devices play a vital role in that research, and they ought to be recognized for their contributions, says Ian Burkhart, who had one implanted in his own brain back in 2014. He’s been working on a set of guidelines for researchers developing brain-computer interfaces (BCIs).

Ethics guidelines for clinical trials already exist. But BCI trials are different, says Jennifer Chandler, a professor of law and neuroethics at the University of Ottawa who also worked on the guidelines. “These are people who have a device embedded in their brain, are in trials sometimes for years and years … [and contribute] a significant investment of time, of the body, and of intellectual effort.”

Burkhart was left paralyzed from the chest down following a diving accident in 2010, when he was 19 years old. Around four years later, he volunteered to become the first person to trial a brain implant designed for hand control.

He had an array of 96 electrodes inserted into the part of his brain that controls movement. The electrodes were connected to a computer via a cable that essentially plugged into his head. Algorithms on the computer were designed to interpret those signals and deliver them to another sleeve of electrodes worn on Burkhart’s arm, allowing him to control it.

The first movements were small, but Burkhart was ultimately able to use the system to pour beads from bottles, move small and delicate objects, and even play Guitar Hero, if only during lab visits. It was a scientific breakthrough.

Burkhart took part in two years-long clinical trials over the seven-and-a-half-year period he had the electrode array implanted in his brain. “It was a fantastic experience,” he says. “But there’s certainly some things that, knowing what I know now, I would want to do a little differently.”

In 2022, Burkhart cofounded BCI Pioneers Coalition—an organization through which people who have taken part in BCI trials can share their experiences, both with each other and with researchers. Over the last year, members of the group have been developing a set of guidelines based on those experiences. The idea is to help academics, clinicians, and companies run ethical trials that respect participants’ autonomy.

The guidelines, published on Tuesday, lay out a list of recommendations that fall within 13 categories. One, for example, focuses on recognizing and compensating trial participants. During the trials that Burkhart participated in, “I was going into the lab two or three days a week, for four hours at a time,” he recalls. “That’s [easily] a part-time job if you just count the hours you’re putting in.”

As the trial progressed, Burkhart says, he learned more and was able to give more constructive feedback on what was working and what wasn’t. He says he was a key member of the research team. Others who find themselves in a similar position might appreciate being listed as a coauthor on scientific publications or publicly named as a research collaborator, he says. Burkhart and his colleagues acknowledge that not everyone will want this, however.

The guidelines also address the thorny question of privacy. That’s important: The public will always be interested in cutting-edge biotechnologies like these—and the guidelines say researchers also have a duty to prepare participants for the possibility of media attention. In some cases, it might be difficult to completely conceal the identity of trial participants.

Things get even more complicated when it comes to the privacy of participants’ brain data. Research teams will need to access, analyze, and—at least temporarily—store this data. Burkhart wasn’t too bothered about that in his case, where scientists were collecting neural activity related to movement. But people who have brain implants designed for turning thoughts into words might feel differently.

The guidelines state that brain data “should be understood as the participant’s personal information.” They are pushing for participants to be able to access their own brain data whenever they want—something that has not always been possible—and want to make sure people aren’t prevented from sharing it with their own doctors because of embargoes or nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) designed to keep findings under wraps from competitors.
“It’s not super common for there to be firm NDAs within a lot of the trials,” says Burkhart. “But it’s something where we want to make sure that that does not happen.”

The guidelines also address what comes after a trial. Around five years after Burkhart had his device implanted, the research team ran into some issues with funding. When we last spoke a few years ago, he recalled how he was told he would have to have the implant removed and could have it put back in once the team had secured funding. (And we’re talking about brain surgery here.)

Ultimately, he kept the implant until 2021, when it was removed after an infection started to develop at the point where the cable led into his scalp. But losing the device after all those years was difficult; he’d regained the ability to move his arm—and then lost it again.

Rita Leggett, an Australian woman who had a device implanted in her brain to treat her epilepsy, has said she felt she “became one” with her implant. When the company that made it went bust two years later, the device was removed against her will—an act ethicists have described as a potential breach of human rights.

Researchers should instead commit to maintaining brain devices for a “reasonable period” after a trial ends, according to the guidelines. Participants should be given plenty of time to prepare for the surgery to remove it. And researchers should set aside extra funds to support trial participants who have to do that.

Some of the guidelines are vague and may overlap with existing ethics standards. They don’t all spell out explicit solutions. They were also developed with feedback from a small group of individuals—the number of people living with BCIs is still very low. The team hopes to grow and expand on the guidelines over time. Burkhart also plans to discuss them with researchers at an upcoming neuroscience conference.
“This is a living document, and this is version one,” says Chandler. “It’s just the starting point.”
This article first appeared in The Checkup, MIT Technology Review’s weekly biotech newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Thursday, and read articles like this first, sign up here.
245deba2bfd0bb29: The self-styled visionaries of Silicon Valley, leaders like OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and SpaceX boss Elon Musk, have built careers claiming to see the future. Long-term vision is currency: Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg built a 10-year road map for Facebook in 2016, and Google famously told investors before its public offering that it was unconcerned with short-term results. And yet there they all were, a mere five weeks before the midterm elections, gathered at the White House to smile for photos with President Trump and sign on to his “Super Intelligence” agenda.

Even by the diminished standards of today’s corporate governance, this was a shockingly foolish decision. Despite dozens of polls showing a rising tide of anti-Trump sentiment and bipartisan rejection of AI and data centers, the futurists of the tech elite cast aside long-term corporate interests for short-term political favor. And now, their industry is very squarely in the new victors’ crosshairs.

For an industry obsessed with pattern recognition, their decision to lash themselves to President Trump has proved to be a catastrophic misreading of the political landscape. Now, not only have they jeopardized their companies’ fates, but they’ve also raised questions about their vision and judgment.

The people who work for them are just as confused as the rest of us. Tech workers I’ve spoken to at OpenAI, Meta, and other firms have noted an absence of commentary from their leaders post-election. Zuckerberg has yet to address the results internally, while an employee at another AI firm said that “leadership has been pretty silent on Slack.” Most employees share concern about potential anti-data-center legislation and are curious how leadership will adjust to a Democratic Washington, DC. But more than anything, they don’t understand how their bosses didn’t see what was so blindingly obvious to everyone else.

In Silicon Valley, the Gretzkyism “skate to where the puck is going, not where it has been” is a management maxim; it preaches anticipation and foresight over reactiveness to the present moment. Tech entrepreneurs love a good “pivot,” and companies that can’t change with the times get disrupted and die.

Which is why I find it so strange that Zuckerberg, OpenAI cofounder Greg Brockman, and so many of Silicon Valley’s other prominent AI leaders and venture capitalists have put themselves in a potentially inescapable political bind. In going all in on President Trump’s cultural and business agenda instead of playing both sides of the aisle as corporate America usually does, they’ve built identities they may not be able to pivot out of. Will anyone really believe that Palantir CEO Alex Karp is suddenly progressive after a year of promising “violence and death to our enemies” and telling investors that the company is “completely anti-woke”?

I believe this is less a surprise than a very public exposure of a fundamental reality: that tech’s most visible leaders are not all-knowing visionary masterminds after all. Insights about social media or artificial intelligence do not make Zuckerberg or Altman experts on politics, the economy, or much else outside of technology. The instant gratification of presidential access, subsidies, and a say in their own regulation blinded them to the basics of political math that they clearly did not understand.

There’s a reason the chief executives of Chase, Boeing, and other Fortune 500 staples don’t go on podcasts to talk about “masculine energy,” or call the president from the stage of a MAGA-friendly AI summit to label fears about AI a “hoax” and a “scam.” This is the learned wisdom of decades operating in an environment where the customer changes every four years but contracts run for 10. Most companies play to both sides of the aisle because they know that their business models and multibillion-dollar projects must outlast the current administration. Instead, Big Tech tied itself to Trump and made its most important goals and investments—many related to grid access and data center permits—immediate targets for Democrats.

In tech, you can always sunset a feature or update some code. But in politics, there is no undo button for failures that change public perception. The tech elites’ decision to visibly align their businesses with a temporary movement has left them no credible way to pivot now that the climate has changed. As one Meta employee who has worked closely with Zuckerberg put it, “Mark is a long-term thinker, but he never charts a plan of how to get there. It’s spray and pray and see what happens.” As for whether employees expect the company to do a strategic postmortem? “Facebook has never really done that.”

“Move fast and break things” might work in a startup, but it’s a terrible strategy for building reputational goodwill. Previous technological leaps, like the rollout of fiber-optic technology and wireless infrastructure, avoided partisan politics. But by kowtowing to the Trump administration, Silicon Valley made artificial intelligence a culture-war issue. Now, when citizens vote on data center proposals from California to Florida, they are no longer considering only technical or economic concerns, but political ones.

Tech leaders didn’t see this coming because they were too focused on the urgency of the AI race to understand how reputational damage could undermine the intangible goodwill—and ultimately the very tangible infrastructure—necessary to win it. The industry’s misreading of the moment has already punctured one myth Silicon Valley holds dear: that its leaders can always see what’s next.
Aaron Zamost is a tech communications consultant and a former executive at Square.

0cc4e4656b42c7c3: HONG KONG, Nov 13 — Stocks mostly fell today, tracking a selloff on Wall Street as traders were spooked by the downfall of Nvidia mastermind Jensen Huang.

Investors were also keeping tabs on the Middle East crisis after Donald Trump called on Vice President JD Vance to focus on domestic issues rather than negotiations with Tehran, signalling fading interest in a peace deal.

Chip titan Nvidia has been sideswiped since reports emerged that Huang — a pivotal figure in the artificial intelligence explosion in recent years — had carried on two extramarital affairs, including with a woman accused of spying for China.
After days of speculation, he stepped down yesterday in the face of a boardroom revolt. He will be replaced on an interim basis by chief financial officer Colette Kress.
The crisis has seen Nvidia’s share price fall about a fifth since news of the first affair broke at the end of last month.
It fell around 14 per cent after Huang’s resignation but rebounded on dip-buying to end a little more than four per cent down, while it was up one per cent in after-hours trade.

While the crisis had raised concerns about the AI boom, which had already been stuttering owing to profitability questions, observers pointed out that business would continue and Huang’s departure would not affect short-term projects already in the works.
A Republican senator said yesterday that Huang had been asked to appear before US lawmakers, as had Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who faces scrutiny over the sale of advanced chips to China.

“Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology. I am requesting that NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick testify before the Senate Banking Committee,” the committee’s chairman Tim Scott said on X.
The firm’s competitors benefitted, with Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices both rallying in New York, though all three markets on Wall Street ended lower.
Asia enjoyed a more positive start today but anxiety over the crisis set in as the weekend loomed.
While Tokyo and Taipei remained in positive territory at the close — albeit at lower levels — Seoul finished down one per cent.
There were also losses in Hong Kong, Shanghai, Sydney, Singapore, Wellington, Manila and Mumbai. Bangkok and Jakarta rose.
London, Paris and Frankfurt opened lower.
Gauge of AI boom

“Now that he has taken the decision to resign, the question that needs asking is whether recent events matter in the context of the wider business given that Nvidia is one of the front runners in the AI trade?” wrote Michael Hewson at MCH Market Insights.

“Business is likely to continue as before and with the numbers out next week the noise around its CEO while unwelcome doesn’t change the business case for Nvidia, even if it raises some questions about its corporate governance.

“These questions are likely to continue to rumble and there is a danger that Nvidia might become collateral damage in the aftermath as Democrats take aim at a business that has aligned itself closely to the Trump administration.”

Traders were also gearing up for next week’s market debut of Anthropic, creator of the Claude chatbot, following an initial public offering that is expected to have raised more than US$60 billion (RM245 billion).

The listing is seen as a gauge of how long the AI spending boom can last in the face of concerns about the huge spending on data centres and software, and possible regulation following the Democratic sweep of Congress last week.
Both main oil contracts edged down today, having seen big gains the day before after Trump appeared to turn his back on a peace agreement with Iran.
“We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.
The comments followed a sharp drop in crude this month on optimism the president would push for a long-standing deal with Tehran after saying he would not restart military action against Iran.

Traders are also keeping an eye on currency markets after the dollar broke back above 160 yen — the first time since the start of September — on bets the Federal Reserve will keep hiking interest rates into the new year.
The greenback’s advance sparked fresh speculation that authorities will step in to support the Japanese unit. — AFP
6c81546677e5d7f7: Only a handful of NHS trusts are using the cancer app on the controversial £330 million Federated Data Platform (FDP) run by Palantir, while newly released figures raise questions about which trusts are benefiting.
Cancer 360 was designed to bring cancer patients' data from disparate spreadsheets and electronic health records into a central system, helping health professionals prioritize treatment.

Pilots began four years ago, and trusts are not charged directly for the FDP. Yet official figures put Cancer 360's uptake at just five or six trusts. Freedom of Information responses gathered by grassroots campaign group No Palantir in the NHS also reveal discrepancies between reported benefits and recorded use.

In June 2025, NHS England said that Cancer 360 "drastically cut down diagnosis times" and referred to a pilot at Chelsea and Westminster NHS Foundation Trust, which saw the proportion of patients diagnosed within 28 days climb from 72 percent to 85 percent.

The trust began trials in 2022, while working with Palantir under a £23 million contract awarded without competition, before the US firm was awarded the FDP contract in late 2023. Critics argued the FDP procurement was flawed as Palantir had developed use cases under £60 million in non-competitive contracts which were then carried over to the FDP.
Last year, NHS England said Cancer 360 served 46 registered teams and 239 active users, and processed 52,000 patients.

In June 2026, NHS England said there were five trusts using Cancer 360 as of March 2026. Of those, only two were listed as benefiting. In July, health minister Preet Kaur Gill repeated the five-trust usage figure in a Parliamentary answer.

Official data released in October said that as of June, six trusts were using Cancer 360 and five were benefiting, but did not identify the trusts or explain the increase. The stats have since been removed from the NHS England website but are archived here.
In June, NHS England responded to a Freedom of Information request. It said six trusts reported unique users logging into the Cancer 360 app over the last 12 months.

However, two trusts cited as having run successful pilots – Chelsea and Westminster Hospital and Royal United Hospitals Bath – were listed as having zero unique users logging into the system during that period, according to NHS England's reply.
Both trusts were said to have received benefits from the system, according to a FoI response sent to campaign group Foxglove in June this year.
The Register asked both trusts and NHS England to explain the discrepancy.

One of the six trusts said to be logging into the cancer app, East Lancashire Hospitals, reported just one unique user. It later confirmed in an FoI response in August that it was not live with the FDP. It had planned to adopt the platform, leading with Cancer 360, but did not have a date for going live with the app.
No Palantir in the NHS also identified trusts that considered Cancer 360 but decided against adopting it.
East Kent Hospitals University NHS Foundation Trust considered using the app but rejected it because there was "no immediate requirement for it," according to its FoI response.
In its FoI response, Bedfordshire Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust said it did not adopt the app because of issues around the metadata requirements.
Meanwhile, official figures on cancer diagnosis waiting times show wider improvements across England. Given Cancer 360's limited uptake, those national gains cannot simply be credited to the app.
In July this year, the UK's statistical regulator told NHS England to ensure ministers are briefed accurately following a row over data used to promote the purported benefits of the Palantir-run FDP.

Campaign group Foxglove had found that nearly a third of NHS trusts using Palantir's health data platform were performing fewer patient procedures than before it went live and that Chelsea and Westminster Hospital accounted for 84 percent of the reported fall in outpatient waiting lists, while only 16 trusts were using the FDP tool. The Office for Statistics Regulation began assessing NHS England's claims about the FDP's performance and the quango included more caveats on its website.

Scrutiny of the FDP's reported benefits comes as the government decides whether to continue the Palantir-led contract beyond February 2027. The initial contract was provided for a term of up to seven years, with a maximum value of £330 million.

Reports this week suggest the government is set to renew the contract, but run a parallel procurement to find an alternative to Palantir as pressure mounts to reduce lock-in to a single vendor and boost sovereign technology.

Palantir was founded with startup money from a CIA-linked VC firm and has relied on close ties with the US intelligence, military, and immigration services since its inception, although its recent growth in the wider business market is notable. ®

5f7b14ff37d005c9: SINGAPORE: Singapore charged a fifth person in a fraud case linked to the export of computer hardware suspected of containing Nvidia chips subject to US trade restrictions.

The firms had reasonable grounds to believe that those servers represented benefits from Aperia International’s criminal conduct including fraud by false representation, they said.

If convicted, Shi faces up to 10 years in jail for each case, or a fine of up to S$500,000, or both. Superphi and NJ Global face a fine of up to S$1 million or twice the value of the benefits from criminal conduct, whichever is higher, for each charge.

738b382586147fd3: LONDON: Faisa Omar applied for more than 500 jobs in the UK and got nowhere -- a slog she likened to "shouting into the void". It took a 10-week training course, tailored to the green energy sector, to finally land her a job within a month.

Her story is one the Labour government hopes to replicate on a much bigger scale, as it prepares to receive a report and proposals next week that would, controversially, restrict youth sickness and disability benefits in order to fund back-to-work programmes aimed at the nearly 1 million young people not in work, education or training.

Britain had 981,000 people aged 16-24 not in employment, education or training (NEET) in the second quarter of this year, accounting for 13% of the age group as a whole and a share that was the second-highest in Europe last year.

Its 15.6% youth unemployment rate is also unusually high compared with the 3.4% rate for older workers — elsewhere in Europe, the youth jobless rate is typically only just over double that of older age groups.
Former minister Alan Milburn, a party ally of Prime Minister Andy Burnham, warned of a "lost generation" in May in the first part of his report into youth unemployment.

Disagreement is likely to arise over Milburn's plans for how to fund more back-to-work programmes against a backdrop of stretched public finances, something he addressed in a newspaper interview on Thursday.
"I'm not saying that any of this will be easy, or that it will be pain-free," Milburn told the Times. "Candidly, it could mean that some people will get less financial support."

Milburn said earlier this year that he wanted to shift the 25-to-1 ratio of spending on benefits versus employment support more towards the latter, and draw lessons from the Netherlands and elsewhere where more young people are in work.
Next week he will propose barring under-25s from ill-health supplements to standard unemployment benefits and also moving them to a more restricted version of the main disability benefit.
But his report is unlikely to rapidly reduce the £8 billion a year spent on benefits for young people.

Cuts are also likely to be unpopular among many lawmakers in the Labour Party who thwarted attempts by previous prime minister Keir Starmer to cut welfare, handing ammunition to opposition parties who accuse the governing party of favouring welfare recipients over workers.
UK employment problem
Michael Houlihan, UK head of employment charity Generation, said programmes with a proven track record in getting people into jobs should be scaled up.

Around 70% of people on Generation's courses found a job within 12 months, double the average for similar ones, he said, with the key being to ensure courses were tailored to the precise needs of employers in sectors with vacancies.
For 27-year-old Omar, attending a course in 2023 at Generation focused on specific roles in green energy helped her nail down a job within a month.

"Before Generation I had the drive but I didn't have the map. So I didn't know how to get into sustainability. Climate change was one of my passions, but I didn't know how to ... find an accessible path into the green sector," he said.

One part of the problem now, according to James Tuttiett, an executive at IT consultancy FDM Group, is that artificial intelligence has reduced client demand for junior staff. He said FDM now had to train recruits for longer before hiring them out.

"You have this silent hiring freeze where AI can increasingly do a lot of jobs that exist in white-collar work," he said, adding that a higher minimum wage and increased employer social security payments had also limited hiring.
Less back-to-work support
So-called NEETs' reasons for not being in work or training vary, but many lack educational qualifications or report having health conditions that make it harder to get a job.

Nye Cominetti, an economist at the left-leaning Resolution Foundation think tank, said Britain's welfare benefits were not unusually generous compared with European countries with lower rates of NEETs. But young people receiving health-related benefits in Britain faced fewer requirements to engage with a process of getting back to work.

Sonja Bekker, a professor of employment law at Utrecht University in the Netherlands, said her city sent people to knock on the doors of young people not in education or work, to offer solutions such as childcare or mental health support.
Vocational schools mean many Dutch pupils are on months-long work placements aged 17, and two-thirds of 16- to 17-year-olds have part-time jobs — compared with less than a fifth in Britain.
Even in the Netherlands, though, the rate of NEETs has begun to rise. Like in Britain, AI and taxes are sometimes blamed.
"We don't know whether it is a long-term trend or whether it is just a bump in the economic cycle," Bekker said.
ca326b32b3ec013a: The next version of the C++ programming language may be delayed at the last minute due to a dispute over a security-enhancing Contracts feature.

Contracts have deeply split C++ technical maintainers. One group backs the C++ creator Bjarne Stroustrup, who is against the technology in its present form in grounds it was hastily implemented. But others are eager to see Contracts implemented, even arguing the tech's detractors are poisoning the C++ development process itself.
The disagreement boiled over just before a vote to ratify the new version of the language.

In October, the Draft International Standard (DIS) of C++26 failed its ISO ballot — the next-to-last stage in the International Organization for Standardization’s approval process during which a standard's technical details are formally ratified by a set of national standards bodies.

The ballot saw 13 votes cast in favor, 9 against, and 12 abstentions, failing to meet the ISO requirement of having no more than 25 percent negative votes. Contracts was the major sticking point for those voting nay.
Contracts dispute

Contracts allow developers to add preconditions and postconditions to code, as well as assertions that check whether specified conditions hold. Such checks can help catch programming errors that might otherwise lead to undefined behavior.
Design by Contract has long been a feature of languages like Ada and Eiffel.
Developers have proposed adding Contracts to C++ for at least a decade, after when they were abruptly yanked from C++20 owing to concerns over dangerous defaults.
But Stroustrup roasted the revised proposal (P2900) that made it into C++26.

“The P2900 contracts and extensions aim to change the nature of C++ and are an existential threat to C++, adding complexity and bloat,” Stroustrup and his colleagues wrote in a paper last August. They noted that the implementation is messy, outdated, not sufficiently tested, and could be more effectively implemented as a library.

Not everyone agrees. Andreas Fertig, a member of the C++ standardization committee, feels that the criticisms have already been vetted and that vetoing the proposal this late in the C++ release process is damaging to C++ itself.

“The topic has been worked on for years and has received a majority vote multiple times in its current form. By voting ‘no,’ an established system, one based primarily on trust and respectful collaboration, has been shaken,” Fertig wrote in a blog post.

The elephant in the room is, of course, the ongoing criticism of how easy it is for developers to accidentally create security holes in C++, leading more than a few projects to adopt Rust. Adding controls might, as Stroustrup notes, hamper C++’s chief attribute of being a blazing-fast language.
Sore losers
Fertig accused Stroustrup and Co. of being sore losers.

“Every ISO standard is simply a set of compromises. Everyone loses sometimes, and everyone wins sometimes,” he wrote. But in this case, “the losing parties refused to accept their loss. The question that primarily determines how to move forward is whether the group can rebuild trust."
Unlike Fertig, Harry Bott, CEO of the C++ Alliance – which maintains the open source EDG C++ compiler front end – does not see the Contracts discussion as disruptive to C++ itself.

“The draft being sent back isn’t a failure of the process—it’s the process working as intended,” he wrote to The Register by email. “That doesn’t mean the process can’t improve. The goal should be to learn from this and strengthen the process so C++ can continue to evolve in a way developers can rely on.”
Where to now?

With the ballot failing at this late point of the standardization process – a rarity in C++ history – the language risks missing its expected shipping date of this year. That outcome may force everyone to refer to the new version as “C++27” rather than C++26. (That’s only the informal name; the official name of this eighth version of the language, should it be released next year, would be “ISO/IEC 14882:2027.”)
ISO C++ working group WG21 is meeting next week in Búzios, Brazil, for the confronto final.
According to a blog post from Thibault Ricord-Marchal, a software engineering consultant at the Paris-based Margo consultancy, the group faces a number of choices.
They can carve Contracts out of the spec so the rest of C++26 can ship. That will be messy work, though. The undo button has to be smashed on a lot of library hardening already done using Contracts.
Another option is moving Contracts into a separate technical specification, where work can continue to refine the technology.
Or they could do a minor revision, vote again and hope the balmy Brazilian weather chills everyone out.®

3cb396d01877c3d2: In Australia, they’re calling it the “Microsoft long weekend” – an outage so pervasive it’s just about made Friday a write-off at organizations which rely on Redmond’s online services, especially Exchange Online.

As The Register reported yesterday, the outage started on Thursday at around 18:00 UTC and saw Microsoft 365 users unable to access email, attend Teams meetings, use cloud PCs, consult Copilot, or enjoy full access to another 15 hosted services.
The software giant says the outage impacts Microsoft 365 services “that interact with Exchange Online and email services.” Services that don’t need Exchange Online remain functional.
The software giant initially blamed the outage on a mysterious “problem that's causing servers to fail automated health checks and become unavailable.”
Microsoft thought it found a fix but quickly admitted “Actions taken thus far have not provided the anticipated relief.”
In the hours since, the situation has not improved markedly, and Microsoft is still struggling to restore service.
It has also changed the language it uses when discussing the possibility that a cyberattack is the reason for the outage.

As of 04:11 UTC, the company said it could find “no indication this is the result of malicious activity.” An update time-stamped 05:46 UTC stated “As of now, we are not aware of any malicious activity that is causing this incident.”

Microsoft’s status page includes only the company’s most recent update, but its RSS feed preserves each missive. That feed tells a tale of woe that we have distilled into lowlights and present in chronological order:
We’re applying infrastructure capacity improvements where possible in an effort to help support traffic in regions coming online;
We’ve monitored the status of the changes applied to improve serviceability and confirmed that change is not taking as expected;

We’re reviewing traffic flows and affected infrastructure to identify opportunities to optimize routing. This includes verifying the reasons for service failures so we can develop specific actions to improve stability;
We’re identifying alternate workstreams that can be applied to increase capacity in the face of sustained traffic management imbalances;
We're observing partial recovery across regions in which we've applied these adjustments; however, these actions aren't resulting in sustained recovery;

Current actions we are taking include scaling up virtual machines to increase capacity and reduce load. However, we are encountering issues with the machines being stuck in a bad state, preventing our changes from syncing as expected.
Microsoft’s latest status update doesn’t suggest this will be over any time soon.

“We’re continuing to pursue multiple workstreams to pinpoint the underlying cause of the traffic influx and advance the recoverability of the backend servers,” Microsoft wrote. “We’re taking a measured approach to identify and repair affected infrastructure to improve the ability to confirm the developed changes were applied. We’re tracking the results of this approach to verify the servers are showing the anticipated recovery and performance intended.”
Hopefully, Australia and other countries in nearby time zones won’t be the only ones to get an unscheduled long weekend. ®
Updated to add at 1200 UTC The latest status update at 12:00 PM UTC admits users are still "unable to connect to multiple Microsoft 365 services."

Updated to add at 1300 UTC Microsoft says it's seeing continued recovery progress across affected regions, with "broader improvements now observed in North America and sustained improvements across much of Europe. We're also seeing encouraging recovery signals in Asia Pacific, although some users may continue to experience intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery as mitigation progresses across the remaining affected infrastructure."
d9dc5db21bdd63b1: Working in tech support can be thankless when gormless colleagues leave you sleepless. Which is why, each Friday, The Register runs a new instalment of On Call – the reader contributed column which ensures your work to keep tech alive doesn't remain unnoticed.
This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Tim" who told that while working for a phone company he once rewrote 2,650 lines of C as a six line shell script.
He performed that feat after being asked to fix a data transfer program that, strangely, included a bespoke implementation of the venerable File Transfer Protocol (FTP).
"Writing the script took eight hours, most of it tracking down the source code of FTP so I could see if it would do what I wanted," Tim wrote.

This story took place before the World Wide Web became the way to find information online. To find the code he needed, Tim therefore used a Wide Area Information Server (WAIS) to search remote databases.

"In those days, there was no Linux and AT&T had licensed the Unix source code to universities with the struct proviso that it never be made publicly available," Tim explained. "It took me quite some time using WAIS to track it down – the security could have been better – and read the code."
Having found what he needed, Tim wrote his script, which ran overnight to collect data from the telco's switches, tidied up the raw info, and uploaded it to a mainframe.
"It would automatically page me if it couldn't connect to a switch or mainframe after three attempts," he explained.
The script worked fine, but the telco's networks didn't. Tim's pager was soon going off two or three times a night, every night.
After two weeks of interrupted sleep, Tim's manager kindly told him to give the pager to a colleague.
But that colleague habitually left the pager at work, forgot to turn it on, or conveniently placed it out of earshot.
So Tim reluctantly took back the pager and endured another few weeks of nightly interruptions.
How many consecutive sleepless nights have you endured while On Call? If you have enough energy, click here to send your story with On Call so we can share it on a future Friday. ®

606399e29c9ee7e9: The use of algorithms to design structures has led to new parts optimized for ultralight aircraft, high-bandwidth antennas, and F1 racing cars. But the best algorithmic design techniques still require lots of computation and time: Users only see the final design after it’s complete, after which they often must start the design process all over again to make changes. That process also makes it harder to trust that the final designs are structurally sound. MIT researchers are making algorithmic designs more collaborative with a system that acts like an AI copilot. As the algorithm is generating the structure, it presents regions to the human designer for feedback. In an open-access Communications Engineering paper describing the system, the researchers showed it led to more easily manufacturable structures with higher buckling loads while adding only 15 seconds to the total design time compared to all-algorithmic approaches. The researchers believe the approach, which uses a design technique known as topology optimization, could make algorithmic design more accessible and manufacturable for a broader class of design engineers. “Right now, the human doesn’t have any agency or control over the design process as it’s playing out,” explains lead author Dat Ha PhD ’26, a recent MIT civil and environmental engineering doctoral student who is now a structural designer at LeMessurier. “For these really complex designs, we wanted to also tap into our brain, which is the most complex machine there is, to solve these design problems in a way that’s more practical to industry.” Joining Ha on the paper are Ferdous Alam, a former MIT postdoc who is now an assistant professor at Georgia Tech; Markus Buehler, the MIT Jerry McAfee (1940) Professor of Engineering; Faez Ahmed, MIT associate professor of mechanical engineering; and senior author Josephine Carstensen, MIT associate professor of civil and environmental engineering. Bringing a human in the loop Topology optimization is one of the most advanced and promising algorithmic design techniques. It uses formal optimization techniques to iteratively fill in the space given for a design in a way that maximally achieves the stated goals. For most applications, the process requires a lot of computation and time. When it’s finally done, the designs can be impractical to build or have other issues the engineer didn’t consider. For instance, some designs might have eight or more beam connections at a single point, which would be difficult to make in the real world. “Engineers are always very skeptical of computer programs, especially if they give you very weird-looking or unexpected designs,” Ha says. “On paper, topology optimization is really powerful and can achieve great, high-performing designs, but its black box nature has made it less widely adopted in industry.” Topology optimization has gotten traction in the automotive and aerospace industries, but it’s been used less to design buildings or bridges, partly because design engineers need to know they can trust the output. “A big limiting factor has been that the design engineer has very little influence over how the design evolves and therefore can’t control undesirable features,” Carstensen explains. “The lack of control and lack of ownership also inhibits its use.” To address those problems, the researchers made topology optimization more collaborative in an approach that Carstensen compares to having a design copilot. Prior attempts at adding human judgment slowed things down dramatically. The researchers’ new system uses machine learning to quickly identify the most likely regions of an algorithmic design that a human would want to change. To train the machine-learning model, the researchers created a synthetic dataset of probable human feedback to thousands of designs that critiqued things like aesthetics, performance criteria, and manufacturability. “We thought if we could create a record of where humans have made changes to these programs, then perhaps there’s a pattern to those choices, which is not very different from other types of machine-learning approaches,” Ha says. Carstensen sees the system as bringing together the best of algorithmic and human design approaches. “The idea is to tap into the brains of the designers and get them to infuse their domain knowledge as the design evolves,” Carstensen says. In demonstrations, the researchers showed their human-in-the-loop approach improved manufacturability and linear buckling load by 39 percent while only modestly increasing the total design time. Right now, the approach only allows users to make structures within identified regions thicker or thinner, but they hope to add other options for modification in future versions. “The hope is that by addressing these hurdles, we open up topology optimization to a much wider audience, not only in industry but also to researchers and students in academia,” Carstensen says. From designs to structures The researchers see their approach complementing AI only-approaches to design. “We are arguing there’s room for both,” Carstensen says. “If you are in a discipline that has a lot of computational resources, you can use the other approach. But if you really need the human input, you can use this collaborative approach.” Adding human input also serves to increase trust. “In some settings, the humans need to make the final decisions before advancing the final design,” Carstensen says. “By involving humans, we can get higher-performing designs to the real world to create higher-performing structures. Because it’s not just about designing good artifacts; it’s about creating good artifacts that humans will actually accept and make.” The work was supported, in part, by the MathWorks Engineering Fellowship Fund, TATA Steel, and the MIT Generative AI Impact Consortium.
666c9ce2ae9f1142: Despite fears about robots replacing humans at work, there are still plenty of things humans can do far better than machines. That’s fine with Robust AI, a startup building robots designed to complement what humans do best. The company’s mobile robot, named Carter, resembles a utility cart on wheels and is designed to fit seamlessly alongside humans in fast-changing warehouse and factory environments. Carter features a force-sensitive handlebar for easy guidance, an AI-powered vision system, and holonomic wheels for instant movement in any direction. As a result, humans can cut Carter off, push and pull it in any direction with one hand, and direct it with gestures or the onboard touch screen. The company’s robots are currently deployed in logistics warehouses and on factory floors, where they help humans while picking or stocking shelves and moving items across facilities autonomously. “In these environments, what really determines success is how the overall system performs,” explains Anthony Jules ’92, SM ’92, who co-founded the company with MIT Professor Emeritus Rodney Brooks. “The robot does some of the work, the people do some of the work, and the backend systems do some of the work. It’s that combination that determines how well your system performs. We believe it’s really important that people have an appropriate level of agency and input so that they’re always moving the system forward.” Collaborative robots Brooks was a faculty member at MIT from 1984 until 2010 and served as the director of the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL) from 1997 until 2007. While at MIT, he co-founded iRobot, which invented the popular Roomba vacuum and went public in 2005. Later, he co-founded the company Rethink Robotics, which also designed collaborative robots. Jules met Brooks as a graduate student at CSAIL in the 1990s. The two never worked together, but their labs were on the same floor. The pair kept in touch after Jules graduated and co-founded the company Sapient, which went public before being acquired by Publicis in 2015. In 2019, Brooks bumped into Jules at a robotics conference. He told Jules he was thinking of starting a robotics software company, which he compared to a video game engine for training robots. Robust AI was founded later that year. The Covid-19 pandemic caused the founders to shift to creating robots that could autonomously disinfect surfaces, but when it was discovered that Covid-19 was not transmitted via surfaces, they had to pivot again. “That forced us to decide how to use this technology we had been building, which was really about helping robots understand the world more fully,” Jules recalls. “Long story short, I said to Rodney, ‘I have an idea. You’re going to love it and you’re going to hate it. You’re going to love it because it’s solving problems for customers that we’ve been hearing about, and you’re going to hate it because we have to build hardware.” The founders had been interviewing potential customers for years through Robust AI’s early pivots. They finally decided on logistics and manufacturing as the industries to target early on. “When people think about automation in factories, they think about pictures of the 5 percent that are fully automated with $50 to $200 million dollar systems,” says Jules, who now serves as Robust AI’s chief innovation officer. “They don’t think about the vast majority of factories that aren’t automated at all. These factories don’t even have a conveyor belt. They are not going to tear everything out and replace it with a $200 million system.” Robust AI’s robots can be phased into operations as needed and offer several workflows for customers. In one workflow, the robot can guide human workers to specific spaces to retrieve items. In another it can follow humans to important spots for loading. The primary workflows involve Carter robots moving things from one place to another, often in large warehouses or factories, where they say human workers can walk on average 30,000 steps a day. “These are huge spaces, so a person might load the robot with things and then need to bring them to another station, but that could be 400 feet away,” says, Brooks, Robust AI’s chief technology officer. “Now the person can just say ‘done’ and the robot brings it instead. How the robots are integrated into the workspace is entirely up to the customer.” Getting work done Leila Takayama, Robust AI’s vice president of human robot interaction, recently discovered a peer-reviewed study of robots in hospitals, which were used to do things like gather dishes, move sheets, and transport other equipment. The researchers discovered that, in many hospitals, a large number of robots were turned off and against the walls. The nurses said they broke. “What really happened was the nurses were rushing with a patient on a gurney, and the robot sees them in the hallway and stops dead, and they couldn’t get the gurney around them,” Brooks says. “The robots were getting in the way of nurses’ primary tasks.” Robust AI’s approach to technology development is to understand workers’ primary tasks deeply and build features that accelerate those tasks, whether a human or a robot is doing them. “We let humans do what humans are good at in the physical world, which we’ve had millions of years of evolution to get good at, and have the digital system respond to that and provide us with all the things that it is good at,” Brooks explains.

c3a1e49c87d8788a: The government of Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs has revealed it investigated Alice Huang, the woman who is an alleged Chinese intelligence asset and had an intimate relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, and a possible entanglement with troubled server-maker Supermicro. US authorities provided only “limited assistance” in the matter, despite Singapore asking for help.
The Ministry outlined its activities in a statement published late on Thursday, Singapore time.
The document reveals that Singapore’s Police Force (SPF) and Customs agency commenced an investigation into Ms. Huang’s company, Megaspeed, in February 2025.

“The suspected domestic offences pertained to potential false declarations in relation to the purchase of servers and other related offences,” the Ministry wrote, adding that the exec “was not investigated for espionage.”
Singaporean authorities wanted to know if servers bought by local companies, but exported to Malaysia without ever touching Singaporean soil, might have ended up in a third country.

It is not unusual for Singapore-based companies to acquire goods that never reach the island, because it promotes itself as the ideal spot from which to run an operation that trades across Asia. Singapore does so because it is tiny – the whole nation is the same size as the five boroughs of New York City.
That small size means Singapore restricts the number of datacenters that can operate on its soil.
Those limits are a big reason why Malaysia’s Johor region, which is under 20kms from the border with Singapore and a joint special economic zone, has become a major datacenter province.
Singapore needs deals like that to thrive but works hard to ensure its hospitality is not abused.
Which is why it felt Megaspeed’s activities worthy of investigation.

US authorities were interested too. On 24 June 2025, the Bureau of Industry and Security, which regulates sensitive goods subject to export controls, visited Megaspeed in Singapore to check the hardware it bought arrived at its intended destination.
Ms. Huang attended that event and later met the SPF for an interview.
That meeting ended with the SPF impounding her passport, so it could keep her in Singapore while the investigation continued.
As the matter progressed, the SPF suspected perennially troubled server-maker Supermicro had a role in this situation.

Readers may recall that the US Department of Justice indicted two Supermicro execs for conspiring to ship servers to China in contravention of US law. Supermicro investigated the matter and parted ways with three staff who acted improperly. The company has denied ever selling to Megaspeed.
Singaporean authorities say they received only “limited cooperation” from Supermicro, so in July 2025 the office of the nation’s Attorney General asked US authorities for help.

“Since September 2025, SPF has repeated this request on several occasions to the US Department of Justice and the Federal Bureau of Investigation,” the statement reveals. “Despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance in respect of the company.”

In February 2026, the SPF “concluded that there was insufficient evidence to establish that Huang had committed any offences relating to the possible inaccurate declarations for which Megaspeed was being investigated.”
But the police did decide that Ms. Huang provided inaccurate information “to downplay her role in Megaspeed.”
“She was issued a stern warning and barred from re-entering the country.”
The police returned her passport and Ms. Huang left Singapore on the same day.
The Singaporean statement shows the island nation wants the world to know it does not facilitate sanction-busting activity and takes even the hint of it seriously.

That matters to Nvidia, too, because Singaporean buyers sometimes account for over 20 percent of its quarterly revenue and may continue to do so. Whoever replaces Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO will surely face many questions about the company’s practices. Singapore may just have made answering those queries a little easier. ®

1ea91ef041981ae4: The state deprived a former governor of medical care despite clear warning signs
Originally published on Global Voices
Image by Q Company. Fair Use (CC BY 4.0)
Read our special coverage on Venezuela’s fight for democracy and the political crisis that has unfolded since the 2024 presidential elections, after the documented allegations of electoral fraud.

This is the first installment of a series by Luis Carlos Díaz covering cases of torture, neglect, and cruel treatment against political prisoners, based on the latest report by the UN Fact-Finding Mission. Originally published in Runrunes and translated by Caracas Chronicles.

To kick off this series, it is worth examining how the latest report by the UN Fact-Finding Mission (FFM) on Venezuela was constructed. Based on 213 confidential interviews with 121 victims, relatives, and witnesses, as well as forensic data and judicial documents, the report matches the rigorous evidentiary threshold of “reasonable grounds to believe.”

Despite the Venezuelan state’s complete refusal to cooperate, the FFM’s technical findings expose a crucial reality. Following the United States’ military intervention on January 3 and the capture of Nicolás Maduro, interim president Delcy Rodríguez announced cabinet reshuffles, released hundreds of prisoners, and oversaw a decline in long-term detentions.

However, the United Nations (UN) found that at least 18 high-ranking officials previously implicated in human rights violations and crimes against humanity remain in key positions of power or military command, including Diosdado Cabello, Gustavo González López, Alexander Granko Arteaga, and Vladimir Padrino López. The core architecture of state repression remains fully intact, providing the structural context for the individual cases documented in this series.

Before delving into the case of Alfredo Díaz, I want to address a question that often lingers when we discuss the UN reports: What is all this work actually for? What happens to a report like this once it is published?

The Independent International Fact-Finding Mission was not created on a whim, nor was it meant to issue a general diagnosis and stop there. It was established by the Human Rights Council under Resolution 42/25 in 2019, with a specific mandate: to document the most serious crimes committed in the country to combat impunity, ensure accountability for those responsible, and secure justice for victims. This carries practical consequences, even if they are not immediate.

The FFM is an investigative body, one of only seven active mechanisms of its kind worldwide. That alone underscores how extraordinary our situation is, and how resilient civil society has been in organizing to secure its renewal on four separate occasions. In October, countries in the Human Rights Council voted to extend its mandate for two additional years.

Whenever the FFM concludes there are “reasonable grounds to believe” that an individual participated in a human rights violation, that finding is preserved in secure databases with case files, testimonies, and evidence. This material is not lost, even if no Venezuelan court is willing to use it.

This documentation has already had real effects outside Venezuela. The report notes, for instance, that a federal court in Argentina issued an extradition request in June 2026 against a Spain-based former Venezuelan military officer linked to the 2014 repression. The court relied on the principle of universal jurisdiction — the legal framework allowing a country to prosecute grave international crimes committed elsewhere, when justice is denied in the country of origin. That officer was named in the 2025 special report on the Bolivarian National Guard.

Furthermore, although Venezuela formally denounced the Rome Statute in July 2026 in an attempt to block cooperation with the International Criminal Court, the FFM’s report clarifies a crucial point: a withdrawal from the ICC does not erase or halt ongoing investigations by the tribunal in The Hague for events that occurred while the statute was still in force for the country. In other words, these reports have allowed us to build, fact by fact, the evidentiary record that may one day support a criminal indictment inside or outside Venezuela. This is why more victims and witnesses should be encouraged to share their stories with the FFM.

With that purpose in mind, reading the case of Alfredo Díaz is well worth the effort. Díaz was a former governor of Nueva Esparta and a regional leader of the Acción Democrática party. SEBIN officers arrested him on November 24, 2024, in Ospino, Portuguesa state, leaving his family completely unaware of his whereabouts for four days. This marked the start of multiple due process violations, including incommunicado detention and enforced disappearance. Charged with “incitement to hatred” and “terrorism,” he spent the remainder of his detention unable to appoint defense counsel of his choice or access his own case file.

What makes this case particularly grave, according to the FFM, is not only the arbitrary detention (a serious crime in itself), but what happened to his health. Before his arrest, Díaz had a history of serious medical conditions, including seizures, an anxiety disorder with paranoid traits, and depression. A medical report from that year included pending orders for pharmacological treatment, a CT scan, and a neurological evaluation. The political persecution he suffered rendered him unable to maintain his medical care.

Witnesses who shared a cell with him reported that he suffered at least two severe medical episodes while incarcerated. One occurred in October 2025 and was characterized by intense pain, muscle stiffness, and disorientation, which medical personnel at El Helicoide diagnosed as “indigestion” and a “stomach issue.” No specialist ever evaluated Díaz, the FFM documented, despite repeated pleas from his family and fellow inmates. Such negligence extends the punishment beyond detainees to their loved ones, who remain impotent to help, forced to advocate from a distance.

On December 6, 2025, at around 5:00 a.m. local time, Díaz experienced the same symptoms. His cellmates’ desperate alarms were met with a delayed response. Díaz was eventually transferred to the facility’s medical area, where staff performed resuscitation maneuvers, but he died shortly after at the University Hospital of Caracas. The official cause of death was listed as an acute myocardial infarction.

The FFM is not asserting that Díaz was beaten to death or that a direct order was issued to let him die. Instead, it points to something that is, in many ways, more difficult for state officials to evade: the sustained lack of specialized medical care, despite clear warning signs — repeated for more than a year — was a contributing factor in his death. This constitutes an arbitrary deprivation of life attributable to the state, which inherits a strict obligation to protect the health and life of anyone it takes into custody.

This brings us to the key connection between this case and the core finding mentioned at the start of this series. Díaz was not an isolated case. The FFM also documented the death in custody of Edison José Torres Fernández, a police officer with 24 years of service who was detained for criticizing the government, and whose body bore bruises that went unacknowledged in the official death certificate.

These are distinct stories unfolding within the same detention system and reflecting the same underlying pattern: people incarcerated with known medical conditions left in a coffin, with no one held accountable to date.
Written by Luis Carlos Diaz
